From that position he recounts his past as a spy and often anticipates what was still future for his past self (and for the reader in the "present"), but is no longer future for the self now narrating. He remarks, for instance, that there is no point now in talking about fear, since he has already outwitted his pursuers and his throat longs for the rope. *Prolepsis can be used just as effectively in so-called omniscient narration, however.* In Spark's *The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie*, the introduction of Mary Macgregor includes the information that she would later be famous for being stupid and always blamed, and would die at twenty-three in a hotel fire.

**Classification:** Like analepses, prolepses can be homodiegetic or heterodiegetic, and external, internal or mixed. In Faulkner's "Barn Burning", after describing the father's violence, the narrator compares this quality with his descendants: the same trait would make them, many years later, overrun the engine before setting a car in motion. The shift from the father to other characters (or another story-line) makes this a heterodiegetic prolepsis; the potential story-line lies beyond the end of the first narrative ("Barn Burning" never mentions it again), so it is also an external prolepsis. Another external prolepsis looks twenty years ahead yet stays attached to the object of narration preceding it, the boy: twenty years later he will tell himself that if he had said they wanted only truth and justice, his father would have struck him again. This is an external homodiegetic prolepsis.

**Mechanism: anachronies motivated by a character.** In the examples so far, the shifts in time are made by a narrator situated outside the story narrated. Compare Joyce's "Eveline". Eveline sits at the window "watching the evening invade the avenue". The man from the last house passes; there used to be a field there where they played every evening with other people's children, until a man from Belfast bought it and built houses on it... Now she too is going away; but in her new home, "in a distant unknown country", it will not be like that: she will be married, people will treat her with respect, she will not be treated as her mother was. These analepses and prolepses cannot be attributed directly to the narrator; they are filtered through the character's memories, fears and hopes (motivated by the character, in Formalist terms). Their status differs from that of a narrator's anachronies: *they do not depart entirely from chronology*. The acts of remembering, fearing and hoping are themselves part of the linear unfolding of the first narrative of "Eveline"; only the content of the memories, fears and hopes consists of past or future events. When the story is abstracted, then, events such as "playing with other people's children" or "being respected in a new country" will probably appear twice: once as events that happened in the past or are imagined for the future, and once as part of a present act of remembering or hoping. Because of this present cognitive or emotional act, the events keep, at least in part, their "normal" place in the first narrative. (For a full analysis of "Eveline", see P43.)

### Duration: Acceleration and Deceleration of Pace

**Problem:** The difficulties of text time are more troubling for duration than for order or frequency. Order and frequency can be transferred fairly easily from story time (however conventional that time may be) to the linearity (space) of the text. There is nothing awkward in saying that incident A appears after incident B in the linear arrangement of the text, or that incident C is told twice in the text, and such statements resemble statements about the story. Describing text duration in parallel with story duration is much harder, for a simple reason: *there is no way of measuring text duration*. The only genuinely temporal measure is reading time, and that varies from reader to reader and offers no objective standard.

It is therefore harder, too, to find a "norm" against which changes of duration can be measured. For order, the norm is the possibility of complete agreement between story time and text time. For duration, no event and no textual rendering of an event dictates an invariable reading time, so equality of the two durations cannot be posited as a norm. Even pure dialogue, which some regard as a case where story duration and text duration coincide exactly, cannot correspond perfectly. Dialogue can give the impression of reporting everything that was said, fictionally or actually, without addition or omission, but it cannot render the speed at which sentences were spoken or the length of pauses. To say that story and text are equal in time in dialogue is therefore only a convention. The convention presumably arises because dialogue presents language through language, each word of the text standing for a word spoken in the story, whereas presenting non-verbal events through language does not seem to demand any fixed rate of narration.

**Revision: constant pace as the norm.** Since degrees of duration cannot be described against the unattainable "norm" of equal story and text duration, the relation between the two "durations" has to be redefined and another "norm" set accordingly. The relation in question is in fact not between two durations but between **the duration of the story** (measured in minutes, hours, days, months, years) and **the length of text devoted to it** (measured in lines and pages): a relation of time to space. The measure this relation yields is `pace`. Genette therefore proposes constancy of pace, rather than correspondence between story and text, as the "norm" for examining duration. A constant pace in narrative means an unchanging ratio between story duration and text length: every year of a character's life given one page throughout the text, for example.

**Mechanism: two kinds of change and four degrees.** With constant pace as the norm, two kinds of change can be identified. `Acceleration`: a relatively long period of the story is narrated in a relatively short segment of text, relative to the norm the text has set up. `Deceleration`: a relatively short period of the story is narrated in a relatively long segment of text.

| Degree | Length of text | Story duration | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Ellipsis` | zero | some | maximum speed |
| `Summary` | short | long | acceleration |
| `Scene` | conventionally equal to story duration | conventionally equal to text length | agreed "equal speed" |
| `Descriptive pause` | some | zero | minimum speed |

- **Ellipsis:** the narrator of Fielding's *Tom Jones* pointedly gives the reader "an opportunity of employing that wonderful sagacity" by filling up "vacant spaces of time" with conjectures, and then leaps over twelve years.
- **Descriptive pause:** Conrad's *Nostromo* opens with a description of Sulaco and its gulf, and Forster's *A Passage to India* with a description of Chandrapore; both begin with a descriptive pause. In *Madame Bovary*, between the Bovarys' departure for Yonville and their arrival there, a long description of Yonville interrupts the action. (Not every pause is descriptive, and not every description is a pause.)
- **Summary:** in theory there are infinitely many paces between the two extremes; in practice they are conventionally reduced to summary and scene. Summary accelerates by "condensing" or "compressing" a period of the story into a brief statement of its main features, and the degree of condensation varies from summary to summary. Nabokov's *Laughter in the Dark* opens by summarizing an entire life in a few sentences: there was once a man in Berlin named Albinus, rich, respectable and happy; one day he left his wife for a young mistress; he loved and was not loved; his life ended in disaster. The narrator then observes that this is the whole story and could be left at that, were there not profit and pleasure in the telling; a tombstone has room enough for the abridged version of a life, but detail is always welcome. The promised detail is precisely the expansion, or deceleration, that makes up the body of the novel.
- **Scene:** in a scene, story duration and text duration are conventionally taken to be equal. The purest form of scene is dialogue, such as the tense exchange in Hemingway's "The Killers" between the unwelcome visitors and the owner of the lunch-room: ordering a dinner that is not yet ready, arguing about whether the clock on the wall says five or twenty past five. Made up only of dialogue and a few lines of "stage directions", the passage looks more like a fragment of a play than of a narrative. In various periods there have also been novels written almost entirely in dialogue: Diderot's *Jacques the Fatalist* and *Rameau's Nephew*, several works by Baroja. Theorists such as Lubbock, Kayser, Lämmert and Ewen hold that a detailed narration of an event should also count as scene, scene being characterized by the quantity of narrative information and the relative effacement of the narrator. The description in *Madame Bovary* of the whole class jeering at Charles's name is a case in point. The uproar breaks out and the shrieking mounts (the boys yelling, barking, stamping, repeating "Charbovari! Charbovari!"); it then breaks up into scattered noises, subsides with difficulty, and now and then flares up again along a row of benches, like a damp firecracker going off in a stifled laugh.

**Example: shifts of pace.** *Sentimental Education* covers about eleven years in some four hundred pages and closes with a scene of street fighting around 1851, in which Frédéric sees one old friend shot dead by a policeman who turns out to be another old friend. Dussardier steps forward, shouts "Long live the Republic!", and falls on his back; the crowd cries out in horror; the policeman looks around, and Frédéric, open-mouthed, recognizes Sénécal. The next chapter begins with a single sentence: "He travelled." A few lines then compress the journeys, the disappointments, new loves, the fading of intellectual ambition, the passing of years (some sixteen years squeezed into a dozen or so lines), until one evening in March 1867 Madame Arnoux walks into his study and the pace returns to scene.

**Mechanism: pace and importance.** Readers often take acceleration and deceleration as indicators of importance and centrality. Usually the more important events or conversations are presented in detail (deceleration) and the less important ones compressed (acceleration). But not always: summarizing the most central events briefly while presenting trivial ones at length can produce shock or irony. In Chekhov's "Sleepy", the desperate climactic act of Varka, the maid and nursemaid, is told briefly within a single clause: laughing, winking and shaking her finger at the green patch, she steals up to the cradle and bends over it; having strangled the baby, she quickly lies down on the floor, laughing with joy that she can sleep, and a minute later is sleeping as soundly as the dead. More extreme still is Kleist's "The Marquise of O": the most crucial moment of the story is omitted from the text. Later indications lead the reader to infer that the Marquise, unconscious at that moment, was very probably raped by Count F, but the text coyly avoids confirming the inference right to the end. In this case an ellipsis in duration coincides with a permanent `informational gap` (see P9).

**Condition:** When the duration of the story is neither stated nor inferable, the analysis of duration meets an additional difficulty.

*In stream-of-consciousness passages, for instance, the narration does not say, and the reader cannot infer, how much time a train of thought takes to pass, so pace cannot be calculated. One can then only compare the relative speed of adjacent segments, or locate the passage by means of the occasional external time markers in the text (a clock striking, a change in the light).*

### Frequency: Singulative, Repetitive and Iterative

**Definition:** `Frequency` is a component of time that narrative theory before Genette had not discussed. It is the relation between the number of times an event occurs in the story and the number of times it is narrated (or mentioned) in the text.

**Mechanism: repetition is a mental construct.** Frequency involves repetition, and repetition is a mental construct: it strips each occurrence of its specific qualities and keeps only what it shares with similar occurrences. Strictly speaking, no event can be repeated in every respect, and a segment repeated in a text is never quite the same, since its new position places it in a different context and so necessarily changes its meaning. Borges develops this paradox in "Pierre Menard, Author of the *Quixote*". The text, ostensibly an obituary of an obscure French Symbolist writer, tells us that Menard's most ambitious project was to rewrite *Don Quixote*. Before his early death he had produced only chapters 9 and 38 and a fragment of chapter 22, word for word identical with the corresponding passages in Cervantes. The fictional narrator comments that the same text means something quite different coming from a French decadent aesthete and from a retired Spanish soldier, the former being richer for the historical and cultural changes in between.

**Classification:** As a mental construct, the relation of repetition between story events and their narration in the text takes three forms.

- `Singulative` narration: telling once what happened once. This is the most common form of narrative. Telling n times what happened n times also belongs here, since each mention in the text corresponds to one occurrence in the story. *Don Quixote* parodies this practice. Sancho tells a story about a fisherman who must ferry three hundred goats across a river in a boat that holds only one goat at a time, and he is clearly preparing to tell the crossing three hundred times, once for each trip. Don Quixote impatiently tells him to take it that they have all crossed, instead of going back and forth like this, or he will not finish in a year. *Theoretically, the more common "telling once what happened once" can be seen as a special case (n = 1) of "telling n times what happened n times".*
- `Repetitive` narration: telling n times what happened once. The central event of Faulkner's *Absalom, Absalom!*, Henry Sutpen's killing of Charles Bon, is narrated thirty-nine times, sometimes with changes of narrator, focalizer, duration, narrative agent and style, sometimes without.
- `Iterative` narration: telling once what happened n times. The opening of Lawrence's *The Rainbow* narrates in a single account what the Brangwen men did over and over for years: their dealings with the land, the crops and the animals, the cows' udders pulsing under their hands in answer to the pulse of the blood in their own. The passage is plainly iterative, and in being so it foreshadows the cyclical character of relations between the generations and within each generation.

*Supplement:* In a footnote, Genette says that his classification of frequency leaves out one further possibility, telling several times what happened several times but a different number of times, because he could find no example. Faulkner's "A Rose for Emily" happens to supply one: Emily and Homer Barron drive through town in the yellow-wheeled buggy, reportedly every Sunday for two years, and the text tells of it four times.

**Conclusion:** It is often said that one mark of modern narrative is its subversive treatment of the various categories of time. On the whole (with many exceptions) this is probably true, but it does not invalidate the categories. On the contrary, *subversion can be conceived only against the background of a network of possibilities, and even within it*, and such a network is what this chapter has tried to sketch. Moreover, while the handling of time can vary, time itself is indispensable to both story and text; to abolish it (if that were possible) would be to abolish all narrative fiction. (For the relation between deviation and categories, see P40.)

## P5 What Does the Text Use to Make Characters Known?

P3 described character as a construct in the story, a network of traits. These traits may or may not appear in the text. The reader reaches the construct by gathering the various `character-indicators` scattered along the textual continuum and, where necessary, inferring traits from them. These indicators, collectively called `characterization`, are the subject of this chapter.

**Condition:** In principle any element of the text can serve as a character-indicator, and conversely a character-indicator can serve other purposes at the same time (this is the reversibility of hierarchies described in P3). What follows covers only the elements most often, though not exclusively, associated with characterization. The same device may be used differently by different authors, in different works by one author, or even within a single work; in a general introduction these differences cannot all be explored.

**Classification:** There are two basic types of textual indicator of character (Ewen): `direct definition` and `indirect presentation`. The first names a trait outright, by an adjective ("he was good-hearted"), an abstract noun ("his goodness knew no bounds"), some other noun ("she was a real shrew") or another part of speech ("he loved only himself"). The second does not mention the trait but displays and exemplifies it in various ways, leaving the reader to infer the quality implied. In addition, `analogy` can reinforce both kinds of characterization.

### The Authority and the Cost of Direct Definition

**Example:** The narrator of James's *The Portrait of a Lady* defines several of the heroine's salient traits in this way: "Isabel Archer was a young person of many theories; her imagination was remarkably active... Her thoughts were a tangle of vague outlines."

**Condition: the authoritative voice.** Naming a trait counts as direct characterization only when it comes from the most authoritative voice in the text (on "voice", see P7). The same words spoken by the people of Albany might carry much less weight and might characterize the speakers instead. Narrow-minded, dull people who call someone "a young person of many theories" and find her imagination "remarkably active" are not necessarily making reliable statements about her: to commonplace onlookers almost anyone can look out of the ordinary, and their comments may reveal more about their distrust of theories and the poverty of their own imagination. When a reliable narrator attributes these special qualities to Isabel, however, the reader is tacitly invited to accept the definitions.

*Supplement:* An authoritative definition can also conflict with indirect characterization. This happens in Lawrence's *Sons and Lovers*, with puzzling results.

*The example critics usually give is Miriam. The narrator repeatedly defines her as too "spiritual", possessive and stifling to Paul, yet the scenes often show her as gentle and patient, and readers find it hard to decide whether to trust the definitions or the scenes. Conflicts of this kind also suggest that the narrator who lends a definition its authority may have that authority called into question (the unreliability of P7).*

**Mechanism: the effect of definition.** Definition is akin to generalization and conceptualization, and it is explicit and supra-temporal. When it dominates a text, it therefore tends to create an impression of rationality, authority and stasis. The impression can be softened if the definition seems to emerge gradually from concrete details, is immediately exemplified by specific behaviour, or appears alongside other means of characterization.

**Consequence: the historical fortunes of definition.** In the early days of the novel, roughly up to the end of the nineteenth century, human personality was understood as a combination of qualities shared by many people, and the generalizing, classifying nature of definition was considered a virtue. In a literature that displayed these qualities in many other ways at the same time, the explicit and "closed" effect of definition did no harm, and its economy and its power to guide the reader's response made it attractive to traditional novelists. In an individualistic, relativistic age such as ours, by contrast, generalization and classification are less tolerated, and the economy of definition is seen as reductive. Suggestiveness and indeterminacy are now preferred to closure and certainty, and the reader's active role is emphasized, so the explicitness and guiding power of definition are often seen as drawbacks. As a result, direct definition is used less in twentieth-century fiction, and indirect presentation tends to dominate.

### Indirect Presentation: Action, Speech, Appearance, Environment

Indirect presentation does not name a trait but displays and exemplifies it in various ways. The main ones follow.

**Mechanism one: action.** A trait can be implied by a one-time (non-routine) action, such as Meursault's killing of the Arab in Camus's *The Outsider*, or by a habitual action, such as Eveline's dusting in Joyce's "Eveline".

- **One-time actions** tend to evoke the dynamic side of a character and often come into play at turning points of the narrative. **Habitual actions** tend to reveal the character's unchanging, static side, and often have a comic or ironic effect when the character clings to old habits in a situation that makes them inappropriate. A one-time action does not reflect a "constant" quality, but it is not any less characterizing for that. On the contrary, its dramatic impact often suggests that the trait it reveals is qualitatively more crucial than the many habits that make up the character's routine.
- Both kinds of action can belong to three categories: `acts of commission` (something the character does), `acts of omission` (something the character should do but does not) and `contemplated acts` (an unrealized plan or intention). Meursault's killing and Eveline's dusting are acts of commission. A crucial one-time act of omission occurs in Camus's *The Fall*: the character-narrator fails to jump into the river to save a drowning woman, and the failure becomes his obsession and the central concern of the text. Habitual omission characterizes Faulkner's Emily, who repeatedly refuses to pay her municipal taxes, for instance. A contemplated act can suggest both a latent trait and the reason it remains latent. In Spark's *The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie*, Sandy is suddenly moved to be kind to Mary Macgregor and imagines the warmth that kindness instead of blame might bring; just as the words are on her lips, the sound of Miss Brodie approaching cuts the impulse short. Sandy's latent kindness, and its erasure under Miss Brodie's influence, both show in this contemplated act. When contemplated acts become habitual, they may suggest passivity or a shrinking from action, a trait of which Hamlet has become the type.
- Actions of every kind can (but need not) acquire a symbolic dimension. In Lawrence's *Lady Chatterley's Lover*, before Connie and the gamekeeper first make love, they come upon a hen with her chicks. Connie cradles one of the tiny creatures in her hands, marvels at how small and how bold it is, and weeps onto her wrist; then, slowly and blindly, she holds out her hands so that the chick can run back to its mother. These acts symbolize her longing for warmth, love and motherhood, everything her marriage lacks. *The Portrait of a Lady* gives an act of omission symbolic meaning. As a child, Isabel knows that a bolted door leads to the street, but she never opens it, nor peels away the green paper pasted over its side-lights, because that would spoil her theory: on the other side lies a strange, unseen place which, depending on her mood, is a region of delight or of terror. She never lets herself confirm that the other side is merely a commonplace street. Not opening the door symbolically suggests her preference for illusion over reality, a trait that later plays a large part in her tragic experience.

**Mechanism two: speech.** A character's speech, whether in conversation or as silent mental activity, can suggest traits through both its content and its form.

- **Content:** In Faulkner's *The Sound and the Fury*, Jason claims to give every man his due, regardless of religion; he has nothing against Jews as individuals, "it's just the race". It is chiefly the content of the statement that suggests his bigotry. But the internal contradiction (regardless of religion, yet disliking Jews as a race) and the latent cliché (along the lines of "some of my best friends are Jews") surely contribute too, bringing out the specious logic common to all bigotry. In the same way, one character's comments on another characterize not only the person spoken about but also the speaker.
- **Form:** In texts where the characters' language is distinguished from the narrator's, the form or style of speech is a common means of characterization. Style can indicate origin, place of residence, social class or profession. In Bellow's *Herzog*, a teacher scolds his pupils with Hebrew and Yiddish words and characteristic turns of phrase, evoking the type-traits of "Jew" and "rabbi". Style can also suggest individual traits. The language of many of Henry James's characters, full of subordinate clauses and statements qualified again and again, suggests their tendency to follow every nuance of a thought or feeling, and the refinement of their intelligence. (For how sociolinguistic codes shape characters, see P32.)

**Distinction: the logic of two kinds of indicator.** Action and speech convey traits through a causal relation, which the reader decodes "backwards": X killed the dragon, "therefore" he is brave; Y uses many foreign words, "therefore" she is a snob. (The "natural" causality actually runs the other way: X is brave, therefore he killed the dragon.) Indirect presentation can also rely on spatial contiguity, as appearance and environment do. A causal link may be present here too, but it is not dominant: a character's shabby clothes and dirty room both suggest his depression and result from it. A further difference is that the first kind of indicator lies in time, whereas the second is atemporal. This distinction, too, is not absolute. A description of a character's appearance or surroundings may refer to a particular moment ("that day she wore a black coat"), but such time-bound descriptions tend to characterize a passing mood rather than what Chatman calls a "relatively stable or abiding personal quality".

**Mechanism three: external appearance.** Appearance has been used to suggest character traits since the beginnings of narrative fiction, but the link between the two acquired pseudo-scientific status only with the `physiognomy` of the Swiss philosopher and theologian Lavater (1741–1801). Lavater analysed portraits of historical figures and studied his contemporaries in order to prove a necessary, direct connection between facial features and personality traits. His influence on writers such as Balzac was enormous. Even in the twentieth century, when the scientific validity of his theory had been wholly discredited, the metonymic relation between appearance and character remained a powerful resource for many writers.

- **Distinction:** One should distinguish external features beyond the character's control (height, eye colour, length of nose; fewer and fewer of these with the progress of modern cosmetic and plastic surgery) from features at least partly dependent on the character (hairstyle, clothing). The former work only through contiguity; the latter also carry a causal implication.
- **Example:** The description of Laura in Porter's "Flowering Judas" uses both kinds of feature. Everyone admires her grey eyes; her lower lip, soft and full and promising gaiety, is nonetheless kept severe and almost always closed. This plain-living girl hides her full breasts under heavy dark cloth and conceals a pair of exceptionally beautiful long legs beneath heavy skirts. Both kinds of description suggest her repression of warmth, sexuality and the joy of living.
- **Distinction: surface description.** Sometimes a description of appearance speaks for itself; sometimes the narrator spells out its relation to a trait, as in "his brown eyes expressed sadness and innocence". Such explanations may really be disguised definitions rather than indirect characterization. This is the case when a non-visual quality is attributed, synecdochically, to a part of the character's body rather than to the character as a whole: "her intelligent eyes" really means "she was intelligent". Ewen calls this `surface description` and distinguishes it from external appearance in the sense discussed above.

**Mechanism four: environment.** A character's physical surroundings (room, house, street, town) and human surroundings (family, social class) are also often used as metonymies suggesting traits. As with appearance, contiguity is often supplemented by causality. Miss Emily's decaying house, with its dust and mustiness, is a metonymy for her own decline and also a result of her poverty and morbid disposition. As with appearance, a pseudo-scientific link between character and environment was established in the nineteenth century: the French historian and philosopher Taine (1828–1893), with his doctrine of "race, milieu and moment", strongly influenced the way Balzac and Zola used environment. The causality posited by the doctrine is, however, less evident in Balzac's spatial metonymies than in Zola's. A close comparison between the description of the Maison Vauquer and its lodgers in *Le Père Goriot* and that of the mine and its workers in *Germinal* would bring out the difference.

### How Does Analogy Reinforce Characterization?

**Definition:** Analogy is treated here as a "reinforcement" of characterization rather than as a third type of indicator alongside direct definition and indirect presentation. The reason is that the characterizing power of analogy depends on traits already established by other means. A grey, gloomy landscape is unlikely by itself to suggest a character's pessimism; but once that trait has been revealed through the character's actions, speech or appearance, the landscape can strengthen the reader's perception of it.

**Distinction: analogy vs. metonymic presentation.** Since metaphoric (analogical) elements are often implicit in metonymy, one may ask where analogy ends and metonymic presentation through appearance and environment begins. Does the rigidity of Laura's clothing not parallel the rigidity of her personality? Is the decay of Emily's house not analogous to her own decline? The answer is yes. But these forms of indirect presentation rest mainly on contiguity, and in the analogies discussed here contiguity is either absent or far less dominant. Moreover, indirect presentation often implies causality within the story, whereas analogy is a **purely textual link**, independent of story causality. Many (though not all) analogies may have developed from notions involving causality, such as the medieval belief in a causal relation between disorder in human affairs and upheavals in nature. When the causal link no longer operates with any force, they come to be understood as purely analogical characterization. The transition between the two types is neither abrupt nor neat, and in practice they often overlap, but the distinction holds in principle.

Three ways in which analogy reinforces characterization are discussed below (without any claim to completeness). In all three, analogy can stress similarity or contrast, and it can be stated in the text or left for the reader to discover.

**Way one: analogous names.** On Hamon's analysis, names can parallel character traits in four ways:

- **Visual:** the letter O is associated with a plump character, the letter I with a tall, thin one.
- **Acoustic:** onomatopoeia, such as the buzzing of flies in "Beelzebub", or looser forms of sound symbolism, such as Akaky Akakievich in Gogol's "The Overcoat", whose name alone makes him ridiculous.
- **Articulatory:** in Dickens's *Hard Times*, pronouncing "Gradgrind", with the movements of the mouth and the muscular effort it requires, suggests the character's main qualities.
- **Morphological:** "Bovary" contains *boeuf* (ox), and the name of Maupassant's mysterious creature, the Horla, combines *hors* (outside) and *là* (there).

Close to the fourth type (though not necessarily based on morphological combination) is the **semantic link** discussed by Ewen. In allegory the name stands for the character's main trait: "Pride", "Lust", "Good Deeds". Zinoviev's *The Yawning Heights* attacks Soviet society through a profusion of brief sketches of such types, among them "Careerist", "Slanderer", "Chatterer", "Sociologist" and finally "Truth-teller". Non-allegorical texts also often rely on semantic parallels between name and trait. Mrs Newsome in James's *The Ambassadors* stands for the New World; the traitor in *The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie* is called Sandy Stranger; the unassuming beauty in the Maupassant story named after her is "Mademoiselle Perle". Sometimes the analogy rests on a literary or mythological allusion: "Dedalus" in Joyce's *A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man* transfers to Stephen the creativity, pride and possibility of a fall associated with his ancient Greek namesake.

**Contrast too can be created by names, often with ironic effect.** Razumov (from a root meaning "reason"; "son of reason") in Conrad's *Under Western Eyes* turns out to be governed more often by unconscious motives, frequently at the very moments when he prides himself on his rationality. "Laura" is borrowed from the beloved celebrated in Petrarch's sonnets; given to the revolutionary in "Flowering Judas" who refuses love, the clash ironically brings out what is twisted in her asceticism. Although "Ulysses", the title of Joyce's novel, is not the protagonist's name, its position as title implies an analogy with Bloom, and the contrast between the mythical hero and his modern counterpart casts an ironic light on the latter.

**Way two: analogous landscape.** As the previous section noted, a character's physical or social environment not only presents traits indirectly but, being man-made, may also cause them or be caused by them. Landscape is independent of human beings, and there is usually no story causality between it and a character (although a character's choice to live in or linger in a natural setting may imply one). An analogy the text sets up between a landscape and a character trait can be "positive" (based on similarity) or "negative" (stressing contrast). In Emily Brontë's *Wuthering Heights*, Catherine and Heathcliff resemble the moors among which they live, just as the Lintons' nature parallels the calm of their home. In Bialik's narrative poem "In the City of Slaughter" (1904), on the other hand, the cruelty of the murderers (and the indifference of God) is heightened by the sharp contrast between the massacre and the idyllic landscape in which it takes place: the sun shone, the acacia blossomed, and the slaughterer slaughtered. *A landscape can also be analogous to a character's passing mood, but that is not, strictly speaking, a character-indicator.*

**Way three: analogy between characters.** When two characters are placed in similar situations, the similarity or contrast between their behaviour brings out traits that both share. The sharply different attitudes of Dostoevsky's four Karamazov brothers towards their father characterize them all reciprocally. Similarly, in Shakespeare's *King Lear*, the cruelty of the two elder sisters brings out Cordelia's goodness by contrast (and the reverse). But the analogy also suggests a similarity between the good and the evil sisters: in the opening scene Regan and Goneril obscure the truth by exaggeration, Cordelia by understatement.

**Conclusion: from general categories to individual texts.** What has been outlined above are the main general categories of characterization. The study of individual texts calls for attention to several further points:

- A character-indicator does not always suggest a single trait to the exclusion of others; it may suggest several traits at once, or leave the reader hesitating among several labels.
- Merely listing the means of characterization a text uses is not enough. The meaningful question is which type of characterization dominates in a given text or for a given character. This can be related to the type of character, the thematic concerns of the work, its genre, the author's preferences, the norms of the period, and so on.
- Equally meaningful is the interplay among the means of characterization. Do the indicators repeat the same trait in different ways, complement one another, partly overlap, or conflict? The result, and the reading process, will differ accordingly, with complexities and nuances far beyond what can be covered here.

(In stylistics, indicators of action and speech are made precise as transitivity processes and modes of speech presentation; the two mechanisms of contiguity and analogy correspond to Jakobson's axes of combination and selection. See P37.)

## P6 Who Sees?

In the text, the story is always presented through the mediation of some "prism", "perspective" or "angle of vision". The mediation is verbalized by the narrator, but it need not be the narrator's own. Following Genette, this mediation is called `focalization`.

### Why Must "Who Sees" Be Distinguished from "Who Speaks"?

**Background: why not "point of view".** The term more familiar to English-speaking readers is `point of view`. Genette held that "focalization" has a certain abstractness that avoids the specifically visual connotations of "point of view" and of French terms such as *vision* and *champ restreint*. Yet "focalization" too has optical and photographic overtones, and, as with "point of view", its purely visual sense has to be broadened to include cognitive, emotive and ideological orientation (see the third and fourth sections of this chapter). The real reason for choosing "focalization" is that Genette treats it as a technical term, *thereby removing the confusion between perspective and narration that so often attends "point of view"*.

**Problem: two questions treated as one.** Genette points out that most studies of point of view (Brooks and Warren, Stanzel, Friedman, Booth, Romberg and others) treat two related but different questions as interchangeable: "who sees?" and "who speaks?". The confusion has its reasons. A person (and, by analogy, a narrative agent) can both speak and see, even at the same time, and it is almost impossible to speak without betraying some personal "point of view", if only through the language one uses. But a person (and, by analogy, a narrative agent) can also tell what another person sees or has seen. Speaking and seeing, narration and focalization, may therefore, but need not, be attributed to the same agent. *The distinction is a theoretical necessity, and only on its basis can the relations between the two be studied with precision.*

*Terminology note:* Speaking of narrative agents as if they were people ("seeing", "speaking", "mind", "emotion") is metaphorical. "Agent" is used rather than "person" precisely as a guard against this personification.

**Example one: *A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man*.** It is generally agreed that almost everything in this novel is seen through Stephen's eyes. Booth says that any sustained inside view, of whatever depth, temporarily turns the character whose mind is shown into a narrator. If one accepts this, Stephen is not only the vehicle of focalization (the `focalizer`) but also the narrator. Yet even in passages where the language comes as close as possible to a "translation" of Stephen's perceptions, verbal communication and non-verbal focalization remain separate. The novel opens: "Once upon a time and a very good time it was there was a moocow coming down along the road and this moocow that was coming down along the road met a nicens little boy named baby tuckoo... His father told him that story: his father looked at him through a glass: he had a hairy face." The language not only conveys the child's perceptions but contains baby talk ("moocow", "nicens"). Still, it is not Stephen's language, and Stephen is not the narrator of the passage, for two reasons. A baby who still wets the bed (as the next paragraph tells us) could not organize such complete sentences; and the passage refers to Stephen in the third person ("him"), which would be unlikely if he were narrating his own story (*though it might be argued that children often do just this*).

**Example two: *Great Expectations*.** In so-called first-person retrospective narratives, too, focalization and narration are separate, though studies of point of view usually overlook this. Pip tells what happened to him in the past: "'You are to wait here, you boy,' said Estella; and disappeared and closed the door. I took the opportunity of being alone in the courtyard to look at my coarse hands and my common boots. My opinion of those accessories was not favourable. They had never troubled me before, but they troubled me now, as vulgar appendages." This records what the child saw, felt and understood at the time, but words such as "accessories" and "appendages" are clearly not in a child's vocabulary. *The narrator is the adult Pip; the focalizer is Pip the child.* (The actual situation is more complex: the narrating Pip also often acts as focalizer, so that the story is focalized now by the experiencing child, now by the adult narrator.)

**Conclusion:** Several points follow:

- In principle, focalization and narration are distinct activities.
- In so-called third-person "centre of consciousness" narratives (James's *The Ambassadors*, Joyce's *Portrait*), the centre of consciousness (the `reflector`) is the focalizer, while the user of the third person is the narrator.
- In first-person retrospective narratives, focalization and narration are likewise separate.
- As far as focalization is concerned, there is **no difference** between third-person centre of consciousness and first-person retrospective narrative. In both, the focalizer is a character within the represented world; the only difference lies in the identity of the narrator.
- Focalization and narration can, however, sometimes coincide (see the "narrator-focalizer" in the next section).

### Types of Focalizer and Focalized

A narrative is not only focalized by someone but also focalized on someone or something (Bal). Focalization, in other words, has a subject and an object. The `focalizer` is the agent whose perception orients the presentation; the `focalized` is what the focalizer perceives. Two criteria are used to classify them below: position relative to the story, and degree of persistence.

**Classification one: the focalizer's position, external and internal.**

- `External focalization`: the focalization is felt to be close to the narrating agent, and its vehicle is therefore called the `narrator-focalizer`. Fielding's *Tom Jones*, Balzac's *Le Père Goriot* and Forster's *A Passage to India* rely mainly on this type. External focalization can also occur in first-person narratives: when the temporal and psychological distance between narrator and character is minimal (Camus's *The Outsider*), and when the story is presented through the perception of the narrating self rather than the experiencing self. Joyce's "Araby" is an interesting and tricky example (see the last section of this chapter).
- `Internal focalization`: the locus of focalization lies inside the represented events. It usually takes the form of a `character-focalizer`, such as little Sartoris Snopes in Faulkner's "Barn Burning" or the child Pip in many parts of *Great Expectations*. Sometimes, however, internal focalization is merely a textual position, with no personification, although readers tend to attribute the properties of a character to it. The classic example is Robbe-Grillet's *Jealousy*. A... enters the bedroom by the inner door from the central hallway; she does not look towards the wide-open window, through which, from the door, she could see this corner of the veranda... From the far side of the bedroom, the gaze passes over the balustrade and comes to rest only a long way off, among the banana trees on the opposite slope of the small valley... and the same holds for almost the whole of the plantation visible from here. There is no personified focalizer in the passage (or in the whole novel), and at first sight the focalization seems external. But expressions such as "this corner", "from the far side of the bedroom, the gaze passes over the balustrade" and "visible from here" imply a position inside the story from which things are observed. Morrissette was the first to suggest, and many readers have since agreed, that the "gaze" belongs to the jealous husband, whose way of seeing "colours" the information the text conveys.

**Tool: the rewriting test.** One test for distinguishing external from internal focalization is to try "rewriting" a passage in the first person. If this is possible, the passage is internally focalized; if not, externally (Barthes, Genette). *It is not clear, however, whether this possibility can be defined in strictly grammatical terms, or only in terms of the more elusive notion of verisimilitude.*

**Distinction: the relation to Genette's three-way scheme.** The distinction drawn here between external and internal focalization deliberately departs from Genette's division of narratives into those with "zero focalization", "internal focalization" and "external focalization". Genette's "zero focalization" corresponds to what is here called external focalization, and his "internal focalization" to what is here called internal focalization. His third category, "external focalization", rests on a different criterion and is placed here under the classification of the focalized. Bal has shown convincingly that Genette's scheme mixes two criteria: the zero/internal distinction concerns the position of the perceiver (the focalizer), whereas the internal/external distinction concerns the object perceived (the focalized).

**Classification two: the focalized, seen from without and from within.** Just as the focalizer can be outside or inside the story, the focalized can be seen from without or from within. The two classifications do not necessarily coincide (which is why two sets of terms are used, "external / internal" and "from without / from within"):

|  | Focalized perceived from without | Focalized perceived from within |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **External focalizer** | Genesis 22: "And Abraham rose up early in the morning, and saddled his ass, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son, and clave the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and went unto the place of which God had told him." He is about to sacrifice his son, yet only outward actions are shown; feelings and thoughts remain entirely opaque. | Lawrence's *Sons and Lovers*: in her heart Miriam does not believe she will ever have him; she does not believe she can be what he asks, and sees tragedy, sorrow and sacrifice ahead. In sacrifice she is proud, in renunciation strong, because she does not trust herself to bear everyday life. |
| **Internal focalizer** | The observer in *Jealousy*, and many narratives by Kafka and Hemingway: the focalizer is inside the story but perceives only the outward manifestations of the focalized. | Molly Bloom in Joyce's *Ulysses*: she is both focalizer and focalized. |

(This classification is related to Ewen's "axis of penetration into the inner life" in P3.)

**Classification three: degree of persistence.** Focalization may remain `fixed` throughout a narrative (James's *What Maisie Knew*), may `alternate` between two main focalizers (White's *The Solid Mandala*), or may shift among several focalizers, producing `multiple` focalization (Faulkner's *The Sound and the Fury*). The distinction applies to the focalized as well.

### The Perceptual Facet of Focalization: Space and Time

The purely visual sense of "focalization" is too narrow. The facets of focalization are discussed below (mainly following Uspensky, with reference to Chatman, Stanzel and others), together with the specific form that the external/internal distinction takes in each. The first facet is `perception` (sight, hearing, smell and so on), which is determined by two coordinates: space and time.

**Space: bird's-eye view vs. limited observer.** Translated into spatial terms, the external/internal distinction becomes the opposition between a bird's-eye view and the view of a limited observer.

- **Bird's-eye view:** the focalizer is located far above the object of perception. This is the classic position of the narrator-focalizer, and it has two effects: a `panoramic` view, or the `simultaneous` focalization of things happening in different places at the same time. Panoramas are common at the beginning and end of a narrative or a scene, as in the description of Sulaco at the opening of Conrad's *Nostromo* or of Chandrapore at the opening of Forster's *A Passage to India*. Simultaneous focalization can be illustrated by White's *Voss*. While Voss himself is struggling across the Australian desert, the reader glimpses the woman he left behind in Sydney. Later, just as the last survivor of the expedition crawls up to a rocky outcrop and collapses, simultaneous focalization implies that the leader of the rescue party, announcing the return to the coast and abandoning the search for the lost expedition, is gazing at the same "desolate rocks".
- **Limited observer:** when focalization is attached to a character, or to an impersonal position inside the story, a panoramic or simultaneous view is impossible. If a character-focalizer is in a locked room, the room itself can be presented through his eyes, but the street cannot, unless there is a window through which he can look out (as in Joyce's "Eveline"). If he later goes out into the street, the reader can be "taken" out too. This limitation explains why Faulkner's "A Rose for Emily" describes the inside of Emily's house only twice: once when a tax deputation forces its way in, and once after her death. The whole narrative is internally focalized by a townsperson, and since for many years nobody was allowed into Emily's house, the internal focalizer can perceive the interior only by "accompanying" the intruders.
- **Shifts:** spatial focalization can shift from a bird's-eye view to a limited observer, or from one limited observer to another. In *War and Peace* the reader "accompanies" Pierre to the battlefield of Borodino, but is not attached to Pierre's perception throughout the battle: once on the field, the reader can leave him and occupy different positions in space.

**Time: panchronic vs. synchronous.** External focalization is `panchronic` (in the case of an impersonal focalizer) or `retrospective` (in the case of a character focalizing his own past); internal focalization is `synchronous` with the information the focalizer regulates. In other words, an external focalizer commands the whole temporal dimension of the story, past, present and future, while an internal focalizer is limited to the character's "present".

**Example:** "A Rose for Emily" is useful again. Narrator and focalizer in this story are the same "person", a resident of Emily's town, but their temporal positions relative to the narrated events show that they are different agents. The narrator stands outside the story in time and already knows the ending when he begins; yet he chooses not to disclose his retrospective understanding and restricts perception to what the townspeople perceived at the time. The focalizer, therefore, is not this resident as narrator but the townspeople (himself included) as limited observers at an earlier stage. Choosing an internal focalizer makes it plausible to withhold the information that produces the shock when Homer's body is discovered.

### The Psychological and Ideological Facets of Focalization

**The psychological facet.** Whereas the perceptual facet concerns the focalizer's sensory range, the psychological facet concerns his mind and emotions. (Applied to narrative agents rather than living people, these words should be understood metaphorically.) It too is determined by two components: the focalizer's cognitive and emotive orientation towards the focalized.

- **The cognitive component:** knowledge, conjecture, belief, memory are the vocabulary of cognition. Understood cognitively, the external/internal opposition becomes one between **unrestricted** and **restricted knowledge**. In principle the external focalizer (the narrator-focalizer) knows everything about the represented world; if he restricts his knowledge, he does so for rhetorical reasons (such as the aim of producing a shock in "A Rose for Emily"). The internal focalizer's knowledge is by definition restricted: as part of the represented world, he cannot know everything about it. Uspensky gives an example from Dostoevsky's *The Idiot*. The same event is first presented through the eyes of the unknowing, unsuspecting Prince Myshkin: Rogozhin's eyes flash, a frenzied smile distorts his face, he raises his right hand, and "something" glitters in it; the prince does not think to stop him. Two paragraphs later the event is presented again from the angle of an external focalizer: one must suppose that some sudden horror, together with the other terrible sensations of that moment, abruptly froze Rogozhin and so saved the prince from the unavoidable blow of the knife already descending on him. To the unknowing prince, what Rogozhin holds is an unspecified "something"; to the narrator-focalizer, it is plainly a knife. (Uspensky places this example under "subjective / objective". Subjectivity and objectivity, however, belong rather to the emotive component, and this example shows cognitive rather than emotive focalization, so the two are separated here.)
- **The emotive component:** understood emotively, the external/internal opposition becomes one between **"objective"** (neutral, uninvolved) and **"subjective"** (coloured, involved) focalization. Comparing Emma Bovary's two views of the garden at Tostes brings out the subjectivity of an internal focalizer. The first view comes before she has sunk into boredom and is therefore neutral. The garden is longer than it is wide and runs between two mud walls lined with espaliered apricot trees, up to a thorn hedge that separates it from the fields. In the middle stands a slate sundial on a brick pedestal; four flower beds planted with sweetbriar surround, symmetrically, the more useful vegetable patch; at the far end, under the spruce trees, a plaster priest reads his breviary. The second time, the same garden is seen by Emma as a place of sickness, ruin and death, an objective correlative of her despairing state of mind. The dew has left silver lace on the cabbages; no bird can be heard, and everything seems asleep; the vine is like a great sick serpent; near the wall one can see many-legged woodlice crawling; under the spruces, the priest in his three-cornered hat has lost his right foot, and the frost has flaked away the plaster, leaving white scabs on his face.

**Mechanism: the subjectivity of the focalized.** The garden is inanimate, so the psychological facet concerns only the human focalizer who perceives it. When the focalized is also human, however, its subjectivity is as relevant as the focalizer's. As noted above, the focalized can be perceived from without or from within. The first restricts all observation to outward manifestations and leaves emotions to be inferred from them: in Hemingway's "The Killers", the killers' tension is suggested by their frequent glances at the clock and their repeated irritable questions. The second reveals the "inner life" of the focalized, either by making him his own focalizer (interior monologue is the best example) or by granting an external focalizer (the narrator-focalizer) the privilege of penetrating his consciousness (as in most nineteenth-century novels).

**Tool: verbal indicators.** When the focalized is seen from within, especially by an external focalizer, the text often contains indicators such as "he thought", "he felt", "it seemed to him", "he knew", "he recognized". Conversely, when the inner states of the focalized are left to be inferred from outward behaviour, modal expressions marking the conjectural nature of the inference often appear: "apparently", "evidently", "as if", "it seemed" and so on. Uspensky calls these `words of estrangement`. (For how modality systematically shapes the "shading" of narration, see P35.)

**The ideological facet.** This facet, often called "the norms of the text", consists of a general system for viewing the world conceptually, according to which the events and characters of the story are evaluated.

- **The simple case:** the norms are presented through a single dominant perspective, that of the narrator-focalizer. If other ideologies appear in such a text, they are subordinate to the dominant focalizer, so that other evaluating subjects become evaluated objects. In other words, the narrator-focalizer's ideology is usually taken as authoritative, and every other ideology in the text is evaluated from this "higher" position.
- **The complex case:** the single authoritative external focalizer gives way to a plurality of ideological positions whose validity is, in principle, open to question. Some of them agree wholly or partly, some are opposed, and their interplay gives rise to a non-unified, `polyphonic` reading of the text (Bakhtin). Dostoevsky naturally comes to mind first. In *Crime and Punishment*, the ideology of the text (or its questioning of ideology) emerges from the confrontation of Raskolnikov's views with his own conduct, and from the confrontation of his views with those of Razumikhin, Sonia, Svidrigailov and the nameless officer in the tavern.
- **Supplement:** a character may represent an ideological position through his way of seeing the world and behaving in it, or may discuss his ideology explicitly, as Raskolnikov does; the narrator-focalizer's norms may likewise be implicit in the orientation he gives the story or may be stated outright. Ideology therefore operates in the story (characters) and in the narration as well as contributing to focalization, and, as the end of the next section will suggest, this may hold for every facet of focalization.

**Mechanism: misalignment between facets.** The perceptual, psychological and ideological facets may coincide, or they may belong to different, even conflicting, focalizers. In *Great Expectations* the perceptual focalizer is usually the young, experiencing Pip, while the ideology tends to be focalized by the older, narrating Pip (Chatman). In Dostoevsky's *The Brothers Karamazov* there is a similar misalignment between the psychological and ideological facets: Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov's psychology is often revealed from within, although ideologically he is an unattractive character (Uspensky).

*Disagreement ahead:* Stylistics treats point of view differently (in the Fowler–Uspensky model of four planes). It considers the ideological plane too broad and the temporal plane a matter of narrative structure, and in the end keeps only the spatial and psychological planes. The two treatments are compared in P35.

### Verbal Indicators of Focalization

Saying that focalization is conveyed by verbal indicators does not cancel the distinction between focalization and narration drawn at the start of this chapter. Focalization itself is non-verbal; but like everything in the text, it is expressed in language. The language of the text as a whole belongs to the narrator, but focalization can "colour" that language so that it reads like a transcription of another agent's perceptions. The presence of a focalizer distinct from the narrator, and shifts between focalizers, can therefore be marked in language.

**Example one: naming.** Uspensky shows that the various names given to Napoleon in *War and Peace* reveal differences and changes in attitude towards him. Early on, the Russians call him "Bonaparte", stressing his nationality, or even "Buonaparte", stressing that he is not even French and so doubly foreign; the French call him "Napoleon" and later "the Emperor Napoleon". As his conquests proceed, most Russians switch to "Napoleon"; those who do not thereby signal a nationalist stance. A change of name can also mark a shift of focalizer within one passage or even one sentence. Prince Andrei, lying wounded on the field of Austerlitz, does not turn his head to look at the riders who, judging by their voices and hoofbeats, have ridden up and stopped beside him. The text continues: it was Napoleon with two aides-de-camp; Bonaparte, riding over the battlefield, was inspecting the dead and wounded. Here, Uspensky suggests, one can infer a shift from the point of view of a detached observer (using "Napoleon") to that of Prince Andrei (whose attitude to Napoleon has changed by this point in the narrative, and who would therefore say "Bonaparte").

**Distinction:** Uspensky treats indicators of this kind as a "phraseological plane", parallel to the other facets of focalization. Here phraseology is regarded as a means of conveying focalization rather than one of its facets, and the word "plane" is avoided because it suggests a misleading hierarchy.

**Example two: "Araby".** Naming is not the only verbal means; the full range of stylistic possibilities has not yet been exhausted, and it is not peculiar to narrative. In Joyce's "Araby", an adult narrator tells of himself as a child (of unspecified age). His language is sometimes coloured by his perception at the time of narrating (external focalization), sometimes by the perception of his childhood self (internal focalization), and sometimes it hovers ambiguously between the two.

- **Indicators of external focalization:** "I had never spoken to her, except for a few casual words, and yet her name was like a summons to all my foolish blood." The evaluative adjective "foolish" gives away the adult narrator as focalizer. Similarly, in "I forget whether I answered yes or no" the vocabulary and syntax are simple enough to be attributed to the child, but forgetting can be recognized only after the fact: "I forget" marks a temporal and cognitive distance from the events and points to an external focalizer.
- **Indicators of internal focalization:** comparing the silence of the empty bazaar to "that which pervades a church after a service" reflects the child's association of the religious world in which he is growing up with the world of the bazaar, to which he gives a quasi-religious meaning; for the child, the disappointment at the end of both rituals is similar. Another indicator of the internal, childhood focalizer is this emotional, seemingly illogical causal explanation: he finds some paper-covered books with curled, damp pages, *The Abbot* by Walter Scott, *The Devout Communicant* and *The Memoirs of Vidocq*, and likes the last best "because its leaves were yellow".
- **Undecidable:** most interesting are the cases where it is hard or impossible to choose between external and internal focalizer. "I imagined that I bore my chalice safely through a throng of foes." The language is the narrator's, but the focalizer may be either the narrator or the child. As the child's vision, the emphasis falls on the world of religious ritual, in which the child imagines himself a hero; as the narrator's vision, the emphasis falls on the clichéd nature of the child's imaginings, and the tone is ironic. Consider too the last sentence: "Gazing up into the darkness I saw myself as a creature driven and derided by vanity; and my eyes burned with anguish and anger." The alliteration ("driven and derided", "anguish and anger") clearly comes from the narrator, and the word "gazing" echoes the opening description of the houses that "gazed" at one another, as well as the link established between the child's "blindness" and the "blind" street of the opening. But is this self-awareness the child's at the time of the experience, or the adult's many years later? The sentence gives no decisive clue.

**Limitation: a more radical proposal.** This chapter has treated focalization as a textual factor related to both story and narration. The view could be challenged: focalization might not merely be related to these two aspects but actually absorbed by them, and so disappear from the analysis of the "text". The argument runs as follows: if the focalizer is a character, his acts of perception are part of the story; if the focalizer is the narrator, focalization is just one of the many rhetorical strategies at the narrator's disposal. *This hypothesis is not yet developed enough to be fully convincing*, but in future it may modify the post-Genettean theory presented here.

**Conclusion:** Focalization separates "who sees" from "who speaks" and unfolds along three criteria: the focalizer's position (external / internal), the way the focalized is perceived (from without / from within), and the degree of persistence (fixed / alternating / multiple). It divides into three facets, perceptual, psychological and ideological, which may coincide or diverge. Focalization itself is non-verbal, but it is "coloured" into the narrator's language through indicators such as naming, modality, evaluative words, vocabulary and syntax. "Araby" shows that these indicators are sometimes not enough to decide who sees, and that this undecidability is itself part of the meaning of the text. The next chapter turns to the other side of the distinction: who speaks, at what level, and with what reliability.

## P7 Who Speaks, at What Level, and Can We Believe Them?

### Who Takes Part in Narrative Communication?

**Background: Chatman's diagram.** To fit the view of narration popularized by Booth into a semiotic model of communication, Chatman proposes the following diagram:

```
real author → [ implied author → (narrator) → (narratee) → implied reader ] → real reader
```

Of the six participants, the real author and the real reader are placed outside narrative communication proper. Within the text they are "represented" by substitute agents, which Booth, Iser, Perry and others call the `implied author` and the `implied reader`.

**Definition: Booth's implied author.** Booth's implied author seems to be not merely a textual position but a person-like entity, often called the author's "second self": the governing consciousness of the work as a whole, the source of the norms the work embodies. Its relation to the real author is psychologically very complex and has hardly been analysed, except for the observation that the implied author is often intellectually and morally far superior to the real men and women who write. In any case the two need not be identical, and often are not. An author can embody in a work ideas, beliefs and emotions different from, even opposed to, those he holds in real life, and can embody different ideas, beliefs and emotions in different works. The real author is subject to the vicissitudes of real life, whereas the implied author of a particular work is conceived as a stable entity, ideally consistent with itself within the work.

**Distinction: implied author ≠ narrator.** Most readers feel intuitively that the implied author of Browning's "My Last Duchess" or of Bierce's "Oil of Dog" does not share the norms of the narrators of these texts. Chatman offers a semiotic explanation of the distinction. Unlike the narrator, the implied author can tell us nothing. It, or better "it", has no voice and no direct means of communicating; it instructs us silently, through the design of the whole, through all the voices, through every means it has chosen to let us learn. The narrator can only be defined, circularly, as the "narrating voice" or "speaker" of the text, whereas the implied author is by definition voiceless. In this sense the implied author must be seen as a construct that the reader infers and assembles from all the components of the text. *It seems far safer to speak of it as a construct based on the text than to imagine it as a personified consciousness or "second self".* Like the implied author, the implied reader is a construct; and just as the former differs from the real author and the narrator, the latter differs from the real reader and the narratee.

**Problem:** Chatman holds that every text has an implied author and an implied reader, while narrator and narratee are optional (hence the brackets in the diagram). When they are present, communication runs from implied author to narrator to narratee and finally to implied reader; when they are absent, communication takes place only between implied author and implied reader.

**Revision one: the implied author cannot be an addresser.** If the implied author is only a construct, and if what defines it as distinct from the narrator is precisely that it has "no voice, no direct means of communicating", then it is contradictory to cast it as the addresser in a communication situation. (It is equally hard to see how an impersonal implied entity could "choose" means of communication.) This does not deny the importance of the concept of the implied author, or its usefulness in analysing and even understanding narrative fiction. On the contrary, the concept is important, and often crucial in determining how readers view a major component, the narrator, chiefly when narration is unreliable (see the fifth section of this chapter). The point is that *if the implied author is to be kept consistently distinct from the real author and from the narrator, it must be depersonified, and is best regarded as a set of implicit norms rather than as a speaker or a voice* (that is, not as an agent). The implied author therefore cannot, in a literal sense, be a participant in the narrative communication situation.

**Revision two: narrator and narratee are constitutive.** The second revision makes narrator and narratee constitutive rather than optional factors of narrative communication. At least in this sense there is always a teller in the tale: any utterance, or record of one, presupposes someone who produces it. Even when a narrative text presents nothing but pure dialogue, a manuscript in a bottle, or forgotten letters and diaries, there is, beyond the speakers or writers of these utterances, a "higher" narrative authority responsible for "quoting" the dialogue or "transcribing" the written records.

- **Definition:** the `narrator` is minimally defined as the agent which at the very least narrates, or engages in some activity serving the needs of narration. Writing a diary or a letter is therefore a form of narration, even though the writer need not intend to narrate or even be aware of doing so. (Chatman, by contrast, holds that a diary may or may not narrate, and that each sentence of an epistolary story may express only the correspondent's relation to the here and now.) Rather than a dichotomy between "absent" and "present" narrators, it is better to distinguish different forms and degrees of `perceptibility` of the narrator in the text.
- **Definition:** the `narratee` is the agent which is at the very least implicitly addressed by the narrator. Even when the narrator becomes his own narratee, such a narratee is always implied. This is the case in Camus's *The Outsider*, which Chatman regards as a narrative without a narratee.

*Supplement:* Chatman's view of "narratorless narrative" seems to be influenced by the linguists Kuroda and Banfield, and earlier by Hamburger, who proposed "speakerless sentences". Fowler, like Booth, holds that there is always a narrator.

**Conclusion:** Of Chatman's six participants, only four are relevant to the view of narration adopted here: real author, real reader, narrator and narratee. And since the empirical process of communication matters less to poetics than its counterpart within the text, this chapter discusses only two participants: the fictional narrator and the fictional narratee. The implied author and implied reader are mentioned where relevant; for a fuller analysis see P9. (For the later fortunes of the concept of the implied author, see P48.)

### The Temporal Relation between Narration and Story

Narration is an event like any other, and so it can enter into various temporal relations with the events of the story. Genette divides them into four types.

- `Ulterior` narration: common sense tells us that events can be narrated only after they happen, usually in the past tense. Fielding's *Tom Jones*, Dickens's *Great Expectations* and Woolf's *Mrs Dalloway* are all of this kind, and it is the most common form of narration. The distance between narration and events varies from text to text: about fifteen years in *Great Expectations*, a single day in *The Outsider*.
- `Anterior` narration: for obvious reasons far less common. This is predictive narration, usually in the future tense and sometimes in the present. Biblical prophecy offers many examples, but complete modern texts written in a predictive mode are rare; this kind of narration tends to appear in embedded narratives, as the prophecies, curses or dreams of fictional characters. The future that the angel Michael shows and explains to Adam in books XI and XII of Milton's *Paradise Lost* is an example, its prophetic character confirmed by the modern reader's knowledge of history. Every prolepsis is a little "pocket" of anterior narration.
- `Simultaneous` narration: narration at the same time as the action, as in a live report or a diary. The narrator of Butor's *La Modification* addresses himself in the second person and seems to narrate as he acts: you have put your left foot on the brass groove and are trying in vain, with your right shoulder, to push the sliding door a little further open... you are lifting your suitcase and feel the strain in your muscles and tendons. *If one accepts Derrida's notion of différance, no narration can be truly simultaneous with action; what is conventionally called simultaneous narration is narration at the smallest distance from the action.*
- `Intercalated` narration: telling that is not simultaneous with the action but alternates with it. The epistolary novel is the classic example, as in Laclos's *Les Liaisons dangereuses*: writing a letter often both narrates recent events and sets off events soon to follow.

**Condition: the duration and place of narration.** The distance between story and narration is not the only temporal determination of narration. In principle narration also has duration (the time it takes to tell something), but most fiction conventionally ignores it and treats narration as instantaneous (embedded narratives are often an exception). The paradoxical consequences of disregarding the convention are wittily dramatized in Sterne's *Tristram Shandy*. After a full year of writing, Tristram realizes that he has recorded only the first day of his life; narration always lags behind life, the more he writes the more there is to write, and the enterprise of completing his book seems impossible. Like its duration, the place where narration occurs need not be mentioned, and readers do not feel the need for it. Embedded narratives are again an exception. Conrad's *Heart of Darkness* describes in detail the ship on which Marlow narrates, and sets up many analogies between Marlow's narration and the story he narrates: both narration and events take place in a "heart of darkness", and a character (Marlow, Kurtz) is reduced to a voice.

### Narrative Levels and the Functions of Embedded Narratives

**Mechanism: how levels arise.** Most of the discussion so far has concerned the narration of a story, but there can also be narration within a story. A character whose actions are the object of narration can in turn narrate a story; within his story a character may narrate another story, and so on, in theory without end. Such embedding forms a stratification of levels, each inner narrative subordinate to the narrative that embeds it.

- The `extradiegetic level`: the highest level, immediately above the first narrative and concerned with its narration. At this level the narrator of Chaucer's *Canterbury Tales* introduces the pilgrims, the adult Pip tells of his childhood, and Portnoy pours out his "complaint" to his silent psychoanalyst.
- The `diegetic level`: immediately below the extradiegetic level and narrated by it, that is, the events themselves: the pilgrims' journey to the shrine of St Thomas Becket, Pip's love for Estella, Portnoy's struggles with his Jewish mother.
- The `hypodiegetic level`: the events may include the speech act of narrating, oral (the pilgrims taking turns to tell stories) or written (Sebastian's novels in Nabokov's *The Real Life of Sebastian Knight*). The stories told by fictional characters, such as the Pardoner's tale, form a second-degree narrative, the hypodiegetic level (the level "below" another diegetic level).

**Principle:** *Narration is always at a level higher than the story it narrates.* The diegetic level is narrated by an extradiegetic narrator, the hypodiegetic level by a diegetic (intradiegetic) narrator.

*Terminological note:* Bal's "hypodiegetic" is used here rather than Genette's "metadiegetic", because in logic and linguistics "meta" means one level up rather than one level down; Genette himself apologized for the confusion.

**Classification: the functions of embedded narratives.** A hypodiegetic narrative can serve various functions in relation to the narrative in which it is embedded, singly or in combination:

- `Actional function`: some hypodiegetic narratives maintain or advance the action of the first narrative by the mere fact of being narrated, almost regardless of their content. *The Thousand and One Nights* is the classic example: Scheherazade's life depends on her storytelling, and her stories need satisfy only one condition, to hold the Sultan's attention.
- `Explicative function`: the hypodiegetic level offers an explanation of the diegetic level, answering such questions as "what events led to the present situation?". Here what matters is the story told, not the act of narrating it. In Faulkner's *Absalom, Absalom!*, Thomas Sutpen tells General Compson about his childhood, above all the time he was humiliated by a black servant (a hypo-hypodiegetic level), and this explains how Sutpen lost his innocence and became the self-reliant, amoral man he is.
- `Thematic function`: the hypodiegetic and diegetic levels are related by analogy, that is, by similarity and contrast. This function dominates *The Real Life of Sebastian Knight*. The story of Sebastian's last novel, *The Doubtful Asphodel* (a hypo-hypodiegetic level), is strikingly analogous to the narrator V's quest for the "real life" of his half-brother (the diegetic level). The hero of the novel is a dying man who has a secret, an absolute truth, to reveal, but dies before he can speak the word that might have changed the lives of all who heard it.
