But the opening of Breton's "Free Union" maps the wife's hair, thoughts, waist, lips, teeth and tongue in quick succession onto a long string of utterly unrelated things: the waist is at once an hourglass and an otter between a tiger's teeth, while the tongue becomes in turn amber and glass, a stabbed communion wafer, a doll whose eyes open and close, an incredible stone. The quoted fragment alone contains eleven source domains; the whole poem may contain seventy-five.

- Applying the Invariance Hypothesis to this poem would predict only incoherence.
- Surrealism was a multimedia art movement that flourished in Europe in the 1920s and 1930s, one of whose main aims was to destroy rationalist and bourgeois thought through unusual juxtapositions. In verbal art this collage technique shows itself mainly as extremely striking, deviant metaphor.
- This is a transcendental, dialectical view of language: using metaphor to transcend everyday meaning, fundamentally reframing our view of the world and of ourselves, recasting all our idealized cognitive models, and retrospectively changing our perception of both source *and* target domains. This is metaphor as interanimation.

**Mechanism: salience instead of invariance.** The core problem the Invariance Hypothesis set out to solve is how to decide which elements are mapped and which left behind. This question can be answered directly, without invariance:

- Idealized cognitive models are radial, with prototype effects; they have central, secondary and peripheral elements.
- The key is `salience`: a judgement of whether the input text matches an individual's expectations and dispositions. It is both a text-based and a reader-based concept.
- In the "hourglass waist" example, the *shape* of the hourglass is the most salient feature, perhaps because it is already conventionalized in the expression hourglass figure and so comes most readily to mind. Mapping this feature onto the target is enough to let reading proceed. The flowing sand is a relatively secondary feature, without salience for most readings, and so is not mapped.
- Salience relates to the pragmatic description of relevance and depends on the purpose for which a particular text is read; at the same time, genre encourages readers to interpret in particular ways.
- An unfamiliar idealized cognitive model is unfamiliar only once; after a few practices of mapping, the pattern becomes conventionalized, and it is then hard to tell which is source and which target.

**Conclusion:** The structural mapping of image schemas is interanimating rather than unidirectional, which allows meaning and interpretation to be dialectical and to go far beyond the surface realization of propositions. Building idealized cognitive models is not a process completed before the experience of reading; reading itself refines and revises the features, structures and domains of knowledge. The Invariance Hypothesis limits our understanding of metaphorical creativity: it lets us see things only one way and cannot explain how language can point to new meanings beyond both source and target domains, the very capacity displayed by Surrealist poetry, science fiction and every imaginative work of art.

*This debate also shows the capacity of stylistics to test linguistics in turn, answering a question raised in P22: what can stylistics tell us about language? The Invariance Hypothesis came from observing everyday, habitual metaphors; the novel metaphors of literature expose its limits. Compared with the conceptual integration of P29, "interanimating metaphor" is already very close to blending, with its two-way projection and emergent structure.*

### Types of Metonymy and the Simile Test

**Definition:** In contrast to metaphor, `metonymy` is based on transfer *within a single* conceptual domain. It stays within the boundaries of one domain and involves shifts between related concepts, commonly between part and whole, producer and product, institution and its location.

- Shifts of this kind involve relations between parts of the same semantic frame and are therefore called `frame metonymy` (there are other types); it has received the most attention in stylistics.
- Metonymy in which a part stands for the whole is called `synecdoche`, as in hired hand or a fresh pair of legs (a substitute player).
- The notation for metonymy differs from that for metaphor, using the connective FOR to indicate substitution within a domain rather than the cross-domain transfer of metaphorical mapping.

**Tool: main types of frame metonymy.**

| Example | Type |
| --- | --- |
| Buckingham Palace is thought to be furious. / The Pentagon refused to comment on the story. | PLACE FOR INSTITUTION |
| Have you read the new Marlon James? / There's a good Spielberg on tomorrow night. | PRODUCER FOR PRODUCT |
| I need a Kleenex. | BRAND FOR PRODUCT |
| The lead guitar has gone AWOL. | INSTRUMENT FOR AGENT |
| There are eight championship medals in that dressing room. | ACHIEVEMENT FOR AGENT |
| The radio said it will be raining. | MEDIUM FOR COMMUNICATOR |
| Othello was rubbish in that production. | ROLE FOR ACTOR |
| Joaquin Phoenix was nasty to Batman. | ACTOR FOR ROLE |
| Three beers later we were pals. | CONSUMPTION FOR DURATION |
| Check the appendix in ward 13. | BODY PART FOR PATIENT |

**Distinction: two kinds of metonymy and two kinds of distance.**

- The interpretation of some metonymies depends more on context, as with "The lead guitar has gone AWOL", where the relation of "standing for" between the musician and the particular instrument he plays is more contingent.
- In general, metaphor presupposes a certain distance between the concepts it embodies, between target and source; metonymy instead raises certain salient features within a single domain and uses them to stand for the whole domain.

**Tool: the simile test.** Distinguishing metaphor from metonymy is not always easy. A useful test is to try converting the expression into a `simile`. A simile sets up an explicit link between two concepts with the formula "IS LIKE".

- Applied to metaphor, the test brings out the conceptual distance between target and source domains, and the conversion is natural: anger is *like* a heated fluid in a container; war is *like* cleaning.
- Applied to metonymy, the same test breaks down: hired hand does not support "a worker is like a hand"; a fresh pair of legs does not convert to "a substitute player is like a pair of legs". The same restriction blocks the conversion of other metonymies: "the musician is like the lead guitar", "the royal household is like Buckingham Palace", "Spielberg is like a film".

*The test works because "like" presupposes similarity between two separate things. The two domains of a metaphor are separate, so "like" can be said; the two ends of a metonymy are parts of, or things contiguous within, the same whole, so saying "like" gets the type of relation wrong. These are exactly Jakobson's two axes in P26: metaphor rests on similarity on the axis of selection, metonymy on contiguity on the axis of combination.*

**Tool: exercise and answers.** Use the simile test to decide whether each example is metaphor or metonymy.

| Example | Verdict | Analysis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Emma Watson has just punched Draco Malfoy at the MTV Movie Awards | metonymy | ROLE FOR ACTOR: the one punched is the actor who plays Draco |
| that was one thousand six hundred and sixty-two beers ago (song lyric) | metonymy | ACTIVITY FOR DURATION |
| the radio played a forgotten song (song lyric) | metonymy | MEDIUM FOR COMMUNICATOR |
| there are already eleven Champions League medals on the pitch (sports commentary) | metonymy | ACHIEVEMENT FOR AGENT |
| Downing Street is believed to be furious about the International Development Secretary's radio interview | metonymy | PLACE FOR INSTITUTION |
| I have other irons in the fire but I am keeping them close to my chest | metaphor (two idioms) | the two idioms have different source domains (the smithy and the card table); holding branding irons from the fire close to your chest produces a comic literal picture. Unlike "the midnight oil at both ends" earlier, this is a genuine mix |
| Burns: "O my Luve is like a red, red rose" | metaphor (in simile form) | target domain the beloved, source domains flower and melody; one target domain, two source domains |
| angling report: top rod of the day was visiting Mr Simpson, with eight trout | metonymy | INSTRUMENT FOR AGENT (top rod) |
| Dickinson: "Because I could not stop for Death – / He kindly stopped for me –" | metaphor | DEATH IS A COURTEOUS DRIVER, LIFE IS A JOURNEY; personification elaborates the journey metaphor |
| Fitzgerald: the passage from heat to coolness is like eating a hot curry with chilled white wine | metaphor (simile) | bodily sensation mapped onto taste; a cross-sensory mapping |
| Morrison, "Horse Latitudes": the still sea ... aborted currents breed tiny monsters | metaphor | THE SEA IS A CREATURE THAT GIVES BIRTH |
| after the Soviet launch of Sputnik, Americans were "Pearl Harboured" in space | both | PLACE FOR EVENT (Pearl Harbor for a surprise attack) is metonymy; mapping that event onto the space race is metaphor, and it is turned into a verb |
| Hamlet: "The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, / Or to take arms against a sea of troubles" | metaphor | FORTUNE IS AN ARCHER, TROUBLES ARE A SEA; source domains alternate within a single sentence |
| the exercise above is a starter, not the main course | metaphor | LEARNING IS EATING, a variant of IDEAS ARE FOOD |

### How Metonymies Arise in Public Discourse and Caricature

**Example one: "prawn sandwiches".** Like metaphor, metonymy is embodied in everyday discursive practice. Some years ago a midfielder noted for his combativeness, playing for a wealthy English football club, criticized certain of the club's fans for not supporting the team wholeheartedly enough. He said they were the sort who would eat prawn sandwiches at half-time, behaviour he thought unworthy of real fans. British sports commentators quickly seized on the phrase, and within months a new metonymy had entered the media and popular discourse: "prawn sandwiches" came to stand for any effete, insufficiently hardy fans, and "they're just a bunch of prawn sandwiches" could be said of any group of supporters, not only those originally targeted.

**Example two: "the lettuce".** The Conservative Liz Truss, in office for only 49 days, became in 2022 the shortest-serving prime minister in British political history. A comment piece in a financial newspaper compared her expected short tenure with the shelf life of a lettuce. This prompted a tabloid to livestream an iceberg lettuce online, next to a photograph of the prime minister; six days later Truss resigned, and the lettuce was declared the "winner". In the years that followed, the episode generated a metonymy of the type OBJECT FOR DURATION: "lettuce" came to "stand for" a short-lived political office. In early 2025, for instance, the Labour prime minister Keir Starmer, sparring with the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, said that if she carried on like this she would become "the next lettuce".

**Mechanism: how a metonymy takes root in the public sphere.** *The two examples follow the same path:*

- *a chance accessory of a particular event (prawn sandwiches, a lettuce) becomes contiguous with a type (inadequate fans, a short tenure) within the same frame;*
- *media repetition fixes the contiguity;*
- *it detaches from its original referent and can be applied to anyone of the same kind, becoming a class name.*

*This is the metonymic version of "from foreground to background": on first use it is a contingent link that needs a particular context to be understood; after repetition it becomes a convention.*

**Example three: caricature.** Metonymy evidently has important stylistic functions. P27 showed that `meronymic agency` is a treatment of transitivity in which a part "stands for" the whole, placing a person's body parts rather than the whole person in roles such as Actor, Sensor or Sayer. As with "the lettuce" and "prawn sandwiches", metonymy also plays an important part in the technique of caricature.

- `Caricature` is a metonymic distortion much loved by satirical humorists: it distorts some aspect of a person's appearance (usually a facial feature) so that the exaggerated body part becomes prominent enough to symbolize the whole person.
- Most caricatures of the former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher played on her bouffant hairstyle and pointed nose. This gradually evolved into ever more grotesque representations, until the nose and the hair themselves became the visual embodiment of the politician.
- The same principle created and sustained political cartoons of the former British prime minister Boris Johnson and the American president Donald Trump, again frame-metonymic distortions of facial features.

**Conclusion:** *Taking this chapter together with P27 and P26 yields a unified picture: meronymic agency (transitivity), caricature (the visual), "the lettuce" (public discourse) and the mechanism of contiguity in characterization (narratology) are all different realizations of the same cognitive operation: within a frame, letting one salient element stand for the whole. The places of metaphor and metonymy in the three fields, namely analogy and contiguity as two mechanisms of characterization, are compared in P37.*

## P31 What Can Corpora Offer Close Reading?

**Background: accumulation, not replacement.** The methods of stylistics are *cumulative* rather than *substitutive*: analytical techniques keep being added as the discipline develops. A thematic classification of all the papers published over two years in a leading stylistics journal shows an article on metrical structure alongside a paper in narrative stylistics and a study of fictional dialogue; a study of grammatical patterning in poetry appears in the same journal as papers on conceptual integration, multimodal stylistics and corpus analysis. No single model can answer every question about "style" on its own (the multi-model cooperation of P22); nor do the models of stylistics have a fixed "shelf life": they are honed, tested and reassessed as the discipline naturally advances.

One development from outside the discipline has markedly enriched the methods of stylistic analysis: computing technology has allowed `corpora` to be created and developed. A corpus is a large, machine-readable collection of texts, which may include whole literary works. The method of wide-ranging, rigorous analysis of large bodies of text with the help of corpus software is called `corpus stylistics`.

### Collocation: You Shall Know a Word by the Company It Keeps

**Problem: a paradox.** Corpus methods can reveal subtle differences in the stylistic fabric of a text, yet their method presupposes comparing the text with electronic data often running to millions of words. Part of the explanation of this paradox is that corpus analysis shows patterns of language use to be not binary oppositions in meaning but better understood as `tendencies`, degrees of regularity and co-occurrence.

**Example one: asymmetrical synonyms.** Word-processing software confidently suggests "synonyms" for words in a text, but these synonyms are seldom "pure", that is, distributed symmetrically and evenly in everyday language. During the Covid pandemic, illness (leaning towards individual suffering) and disease (leaning towards a pathological entity) were usually treated as interchangeable synonyms. But the verbs that `collocate` with the two nouns as direct objects tell another story:

| Collocating verbs | Distribution |
| --- | --- |
| treat, prevent, cause | frequently co-occur with both nouns |
| battle, suffer | heavily biased towards illness |
| spread, transmit | co-occur mainly with disease |

So the two can be called synonyms, but only on the understanding that their distribution and meaning are not wholly symmetrical. And this conclusion rests not on intuitive guesses about language but on empirical evidence from a corpus containing more than six million occurrences of the two words. *Distribution is itself meaning: illness is something *undergone*, disease something that *spreads*; the former belongs to persons, the latter to populations.*

**Example two: "treacherous" weather.** What does English treacherous mean? People will confidently say that it describes people or characters as "disloyal", "dangerous" or "untrustworthy". But in December 2011, when Britain suffered a prolonged cold snap, a stylistician met the word 23 times in the British media within a month, almost always applied to the weather: "UK prepares for treacherous weather conditions", "many roads across north Wales remained treacherous", "Treacherous black ice causes travel chaos".

- The sense of the word has evidently shifted towards a broader metaphorical use, capturing the menace and danger of the weather rather than of people. This metaphorical sense may even have become the dominant use, but more evidence would be needed to support that hypothesis.
- Gathering evidence to test hypotheses of this kind, that is, examining the meanings of words in contexts of everyday use, is precisely the task of the corpus approach.
- Years later the same metaphorical principle remains firm: in heavy snow in January 2025, when three airports in the north of England closed, the ice on the runways was still described as treacherous.

*This example and the "novel cannot stay novel for ever" of P30 are two ends of the same process: there, a creative metaphor settles into an idiom; here, a word's metaphorical sense may crowd out its literal sense through frequent use. Corpora allow such change to be measured, not merely sensed.*

**Background: Firth's maxim.** Corpus stylistics is technically modern but continues in spirit a long linguistic tradition. The famous maxim of the linguist **J. R. Firth** is: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps." Since the late 1950s the importance of collocation (the company a word keeps) has been at the forefront of neo-Firthian linguistics. This has far-reaching implications for stylistic analysis: to talk about the "meaning" of a stretch of language depends on how real people actually use it, in coherent patterns of discourse and in real contexts of use.

**Condition: the historicity of meaning.** The historical development of linguistic forms in different speech communities is clearly also relevant to our understanding of their meaning. James II, on first seeing Sir Christopher Wren's new cathedral, is said to have used three approving adjectives: amusing, awful and artificial. At the end of the seventeenth century they meant respectively "arresting", "awe-inspiring" and "showing skill", whereas today they mean "funny", "terrible" and "man-made". *This reminds us that testing the sense of words in historical texts against a contemporary corpus may lead to wrong conclusions; the reference corpus must match the period of the text analysed. The last section of this chapter returns to this point.*

**Tool: two stylistic uses of corpora.**

| Use | Procedure | Question answered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| general corpus as reference | compare patterns in the literary text with patterns in a general language corpus | does the usage here depart from "everyday" language? Any discussion of foregrounding or deviation ultimately rests on some quantitative observation of what is "normal" (P26) |
| literary works themselves as the corpus | such as a writer's complete works, often running to millions of words | gives an evidence-based description of a writer's style with a retrievable procedure, and sometimes challenges received critical opinion about a writer's technique |

**Tool: commonly used corpora.**

| Corpus | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| British National Corpus (BNC) | one hundred million words; the website opens some functions to unregistered users |
| Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA) | freely searchable, four hundred and fifty million words |
| Early English Books Online (EEBO) | a large archive of early documents, presented as far as possible in facsimiles of their original form |
| International Corpus of English (ICE) | includes world varieties such as Indian, Canadian and New Zealand English |
| WebCorp | extracts linguistic data from the internet; better suited to corpus research than ordinary search engines |
| Sketch Engine | usually requires an academic institutional subscription |

**Definition: lemma.** Searches must take into account the different grammatical forms of the same lexeme, that is, the `lemma`. The lemma is the form conventionally chosen to represent a lexeme, the default headword in a dictionary. To examine occurrences of the verb choose in a corpus, one must also take into account the grammatical variants chose, choosing and chosen.

### Reading a Key Word in Context Concordance

**Definition: Key Word in Context.** Examining collocation means attaching a specified amount of text to either side of the search word, displaying a "co-textual" window around the key word. The results are arranged vertically in alphabetical order, horizontally usually in sequences of nine to fifteen words. This format is called `Key Word in Context` (KWIC), and the repeated combinations and collocations it displays give persuasive insight into the company a word "really" keeps.

- The far left of the results window gives source information for each example: whether the data are spoken or written, and to which register or discourse genre they belong.
- The KWIC format gives the analyst a bird's-eye view of a word in context without having to read through the many texts from which the data come.

**Distinction: two kinds of "key word".** *Beginners easily confuse two concepts of the same name. The "key word" in KWIC is simply the search word chosen by the analyst, with no statistical meaning; the **`keyword`** in the corpus comparisons of the fourth section of this chapter is a statistical result: a word whose frequency is significantly higher than in a reference corpus, with the degree of significance measured by indices such as the log-likelihood (LL) value. The former is the starting point of a search, the latter its result.*

**Condition: choosing the right window.** How much text to specify around the search word needs careful, selective consideration. Searching for the very common lemma warm yields overwhelming results: 33,495 occurrences in COCA. Adding just the preposition to, forming the collocation warm to, cuts the occurrences to 323. Some of the first eleven results:

| Left context | Search item | Right context |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The real key is get the water | warm to | 105, 110 degrees, mix it in your mixer |
| than any hit since Titanic, but it's hard to | warm to | a business franchise |
| After all she says, who wouldn't | warm to | a story that celebrates the magic of love |
| call them lesbians if they didn't | warm to | amorous advances |
| Not a tear; it was too | warm to | be a tear |

**Mechanism: what can be read from the concordance lines.**

- Vertical alphabetical ordering begins only after all the numerical collocations have been listed.
- The KWIC format does not respect grammatical boundaries: in some concordance lines to actually marks the start of a new clause and does not really belong to the search phrase (as in "too warm to be a tear").
- Warm is a verb in some places and an adjective in others.
- Some verbal uses are literal, referring to heating liquid; others are non-literal, idiomatic uses, as in "if they didn't warm to amorous advances". The experiential basis of the latter comes from the workings of the human body, so it is metaphorical, here expressing the conventional metaphor INTIMACY IS HEAT (P30).

*Reading concordance lines is itself an analytical skill: the machine merely aligns strings, and it is the analyst who must judge which lines share a use, which should be excluded, and which are literal and which metaphorical. This is the concrete meaning of "making the computer work for the analyst" below.*

**Definition: hapax legomenon.** A word need not itself be a striking coinage or unique invention. If it is, it may well be a `hapax legomenon`, a word or expression occurring only once. An online search for brightwindbridled, the compound describing the beating of the waves in the "Proteus" episode of Joyce's *Ulysses*, returns only the word itself: either in electronic editions of the novel or in scholarly commentary on the episode. Corpus tools can at least detect the uniqueness of literary hapaxes, but they really come into their own when examining patterned combinations of much more ordinary words.

**Tool: testing intuitive judgements with concordances.** Widdowson's two analyses in P23 can be re-examined with KWIC:

- The end of Frost's "Dust of Snow": "And saved some part / Of a day I had rued". Given the poet's nationality, a corpus of American English is preferable. The sequence and saved some is uncommon relative to the size of the corpus. One can examine the collocates to the right of some to see what meaning it usually acquires; search rued on its own to see what words usually follow it, how many times day occurs within a ten-word span, and whether it ever occurs at the end of a sentence as in Frost's poem. *If the corpus evidence shows Frost using fairly plain vocabulary in a fairly plain way, the peculiarity of the poem is more likely to lie in grammatical position than in vocabulary.*
- Tennyson's "bald street" and "blank day" in *In Memoriam*. Do the common collocates of bald all carry the feature "+animate"? How does bald as an adjectival modifier *actually* behave in a corpus? Are there unexpected, perhaps figurative combinations? Does corpus analysis support Widdowson's description of these structures as "deviant"? *The existence in everyday language of collocations such as bald tyres and bald statement may weaken the claim that selection restrictions are violated. This is exactly the test left over from P23.*

### Semantic Prosody: The Attitudes Words Carry

**Example: "he / she was approached".** The two sequences below are structurally identical passive clauses, differing only in the gender of the subject pronoun: He was approached ... and She was approached .... But when these structures are extracted from a corpus, there is much more to it.

| Structure | Typical instances in the corpus | Consequence for the referent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| He was approached | by the director Danny Boyle; by the global accountancy firm PricewaterhouseCoopers; about taking over at Stamford Bridge next season | some advantage or benefit |
| She was approached | by a man who snatched her bag; by a pervert in Cork city centre; by three men who attacked her | often alarming harm |

**Condition: counter-examples do not overturn a tendency.** This is not an absolute distinction: the corpus also contains examples of women benefiting, such as being approached to model at the age of fifteen. But this counter-example does not mean the whole argument collapses. Corpus analysis is designed to show trends, broad tendencies and recurrent patterns across large quantities of linguistic data; the evidence it provides is not confined to what may be a "one-off" occurrence of a feature. *This is the same statistical concept as the "norm" of foregrounding in P26: a norm is a tendency, not a rule without exceptions.*

**Definition: semantic prosody.** `Semantic prosody` is another important development in corpus stylistics. It is a meaning established through the repeated occurrence nearby of a consistent series of collocates.

- "Prosody" here refers not to intonation or metrical verse but to the attitude, positive or negative, that a speaker or writer expresses towards the situation conveyed by a repeated linguistic pattern.
- This meaning is collocational, because it comes from the company a word keeps; it is also *covert* and *subtextual*, because it comes not from the conventional meaning of the word but from its high-frequency collocates nearby.
- The discussion of lavish in P23 and of was approached above are already simple characterizations of semantic prosody.

**Example: "natural justice".** At first sight natural justice is a good thing, its dispensers good citizens and its recipients clear beneficiaries. But corpus analysis shows the contexts of its use to be less straightforward.

- Although it is a desirable outcome, in almost all the judgements reported in newspapers natural justice is *not* the outcome: it is something refused or withheld.
- Legal textbooks present the concept unproblematically as the natural aim of judicial procedure, whereas in newspaper reports its most frequent collocates are denied and breached.
- At a corpus linguistics workshop in 2023, undergraduates using Sketch Engine showed that the phrase is not only still active in media discourse but still shows the same negative semantic prosody.

**Consequence: semantic prosody and the "difference" of literature.** The stylistic application of the theory of semantic prosody is useful: on the one hand it supports seeing literature as *difference*; on the other it helps explore the *subtext* of literary creation.

**Example: Yeats's "I sought a theme".** The opening clause of Yeats's "The Circus Animals' Desertion" (1939), "I sought a theme", has been claimed to be a marked departure from the ordinary use of the phrase sought a. How can this bold claim be demonstrated?

- In a 44.5-million-word corpus of *The Times*, sought a occurs 79 times. In every instance, despite the preceding indefinite article, what is sought is highly specific: Buckingham Palace sought a correction; a young couple sought a mortgage; he sought a court order; she sought a divorce.
- Unlike Yeats's formulation, the object sought in the corpus is always single, tangible and concrete.
- The object sought in Yeats's poem is elusive; as the poem proceeds, the search for "a theme" proves futile, and the poet's insistent search for the unknown and unknowable leads to a creative impasse.

*What semantic prosody analysis reveals here is not a rare word but an entirely ordinary phrase used in an anomalous collocational environment. This is a deviation without any surface anomaly, visible only against the background of large quantities of data. Widdowson's remark in P23 that much literature shows no obvious linguistic oddity is answered here by a tool that can capture such "non-odd deviations".*

**Example: testing conceptual metaphor with a corpus.** Corpus methods are well suited to studying metaphor in literature, though this may not seem so at first, since identifying source and target domains seems to depend on the analyst's careful intuition. **Elena Semino** examined the collocates of rich in a subcorpus of the British National Corpus in order to test the metaphor A PURPOSEFUL LIFE IS A BUSINESS, embodied in everyday expressions such as "She has a rich life" and "It is time to take stock of my life".

- Of 139 instances, 7 were personal names and were excluded.
- Of the remaining 132, 61 were non-metaphorical, genuinely referring to monetary wealth (as in "the Tories for the rich, Labour for the poor").
- The rest were metaphorical: a national park rich in wildlife; the rich culture of an architectural heritage; a rich reserve of good will; a voice high in pitch but rich in timbre.
- In these examples rich not only always expresses positive evaluation but, across a variety of target domains, means abundance and plenitude. The phrase rich life is not even among the top fifty collocates of rich in the British National Corpus.

**Conclusion:** If a conceptual metaphor such as A PURPOSEFUL LIFE IS A BUSINESS really exists, evidence for it must be sought elsewhere. *This is an example of corpora testing cognitive theory in turn, echoing the way literature tested the Invariance Hypothesis in P30: conceptual metaphor theory often starts from a few invented or selected examples, while the corpus asks whether, in actual use, these expressions really are distributed that way.*

**Tool: testing the novelty of metaphor with a corpus.** The principle of concretization in P30 holds that the conventional direction of metaphorical mapping runs from the abstract and experiential to the concrete and bodily. Accordingly, new things in society (such as new developments in design and technology) tend to be mapped through metaphors with people, even flesh and blood, as the source domain: a Second World War manual of military equipment calls the new Sherman tank down-to-earth, masculine and the backbone of the campaign; Spender's "The Pylons" likens pylons to "nude, giant girls". Against this conventional direction, the mappings of Ted Hughes's "Thrushes" and Seamus Heaney's "Trout" run *the other way*: nature is mapped through the vocabulary of technology and weaponry, the thrush's days having a bullet-like, automatic purpose, the trout being a fat gun-barrel with a muzzle that can fire tracer.

- These words can be searched in a broader corpus to see what they usually collocate with and in what discourses they occur, so as to assess how far the metaphorical transfer in the two poems is novel.
- This also reopens the question of P26: if the corpus shows that Hughes's and Heaney's vocabulary is closer to certain obviously "non-poetic" discourse genres, why are they acknowledged as two of the greatest creative writers of the twentieth century? *The answer lies precisely in the "literariness" of P26: creativity lies not in where the vocabulary comes from but in what mapping it is placed in, and what meaning thereby arises.*

### Author Corpora: Dickens and Lawrence

**Example one: Dickens's as if.** In an extensive, corpus-assisted analysis of Dickens's works, **Michaela Mahlberg** never loses sight of the "why" of Dickens's distinctive and striking literary technique.

- **Data**: Dickens's own 23 works, plus 29 texts by other nineteenth-century writers as a reference.
- **Framing questions**: the relationship between language, characterization and the creation of fictional worlds, the core questions of stylistics, remains the cornerstone of the study throughout.
- **The critical judgement tested**: earlier stylistic work held that Dickens characterizes from the outside in a style of "grim grotesque": without psychological explanation, but with intense attention to characters' bodily peculiarities (for the question of external perspective see P35). A corpus-assisted approach can test such generalizations, because it mines the text deeply as a whole, looking for markers of this stylistic tendency.
- **Findings**: as if is associated with the narrator's voice and is frequently used to refer to characters' body language and appearance. Within a five-word span to its left, certain types of action verb and body-part noun predominate: Mr Barkis turns his eyes on the narrator *as if* seeking agreement; someone purses his lips *as if* about to whistle; Mr Slackbridge shakes his head *as if* to shake it off.
- Another related pattern is the lemma look as a left collocate of as if, which in Dickens's prose foregrounds the sense that external description takes precedence over psychological explanation. Look often describes how something appears on a character's face rather than a conscious movement of the eyes: Ralph looks *as if* he does not fully understand the remark.

**Consequence: bird's-eye view and detail.** These data evidently ground and consolidate the perhaps vaguer impressions of style we intuit from literary texts. But the key impact of this approach is that it instantly provides a bird's-eye view of a writer's entire output: the few examples above come from five different, mostly very long novels. A curious feature of corpus methods is that they provide at once the micro-detail of a text's construction and the broader linguistic patterns that often escape direct observation. *For a synthesis of the corpus study of Dickens with the "fog" of P24 and with biographical and critical rereadings of him, see P44.*

**Example two: Lawrence's colours.**

**Background: tools and corpus.** One problem with many corpus stylistic analyses is that readers find it hard to replicate their methods, because corpora are protected by paywalls or expensive institutional subscriptions. The Modernist Literature Project corpus (established in 2022) addresses this problem:

- It contains modernist prose fiction, shorter prose and poetry that has entered the public domain: by the end of 2024, 328 works by 31 authors, more than twenty million words.
- It comes with part-of-speech (POS) and semantic (SEM) tagging generated with the Wmatrix tool. POS tagging can distinguish dance as a noun in "She went to the dance" from dance as a verb in "She danced alone", and can identify multi-word expressions.
- Semantic tagging is based on a hierarchical framework of 21 major discourse fields, with the words in each semantic domain including synonyms, antonyms and hyponyms; plus and minus signs mark positive and negative positions on a semantic scale: pain, for example, is tagged B2- (disease), and recovered and strapping B2+ (health).

**Evidence: overused semantic domains.** Lawrence's ten novels were published between 1911 and 1928, totalling over 1.4 million words. **Suzanne McClure** built for them a specialized reference corpus reflecting the language of written prose of the same period, containing 85 novels and over 8.2 million words. Compared with the reference corpus, the top ten overused semantic domains in the Lawrence corpus are:

| Semantic domain | Relative frequency in Lawrence | Relative frequency in reference corpus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| colour and colour patterns | 0.74% | 0.42% |
| darkness | 0.18% | 0.05% |
| anatomy and physiology | 1.72% | 1.26% |
| plants | 0.41% | 0.23% |
| temperature: hot / on fire | 0.22% | 0.11% |
| moving, coming and going | 2.17% | 1.82% |
| living creatures: animals, birds etc. | 0.42% | 0.28% |
| speech: communicative | 1.26% | 1.02% |
| size: small | 0.27% | 0.17% |
| sound: quiet | 0.17% | 0.09% |

Colour and colour patterns is the most marked difference between Lawrence and his contemporaries: this category has 10,604 words, 0.74% of the Lawrence corpus, against only 0.42% in the reference corpus.

**Evidence: colour-concept keywords.** Ranked by log-likelihood (LL), the top eleven colour-concept keywords are: dark 1,936, darkness 529, pale 356, ruddy 138, scarlet 121, glistening 96, luminous 62, gleaming 58, dusky 56, glisten 54, bluish 48.

- The top-ranked word is dark, with darkness second. The recurring theme of light and dark in Lawrence's novels is associated with conceptual colour keywords such as luminous, gleaming and dusky.
- Lawrence tends to use several colour descriptors within a single (albeit syntactically complex) sentence. A sentence from *Women in Love*:

> In the large *darkish* kitchen of the mill, the labourer's wife was talking shrilly to Hermione and Gerald, who stood, he in *white* and she in a *glistening bluish* foulard, strangely *luminous* in the *dusk* of the room; whilst from the cages on the walls, a dozen or more canaries sang at the top of their voices.

**Example: the case of "scarlet".** Scarlet is the only true colour word in the keyword list.

- The computer's own file-search function is enough to show that scarlet occurs at least once in each of Lawrence's ten novels. One advantage of text files is that the surrounding context is easy to capture. A passage in *Lady Chatterley's Lover* suggests that if men wore *scarlet* trousers they would not think so much about money; if they could dance, sing, swagger and be handsome, they would need very little of it. The context expresses more clearly Lawrence's belief in the poles of "being" and "living", his distaste for material wealth, and the traditional binary of male and female.
- Analysis with the concordance function of WordSmith shows that scarlet occurs 144 times in the ten novels, its main collocates including feather, flowers and fringe. The concordance lines show Lawrence often using the word in describing the colours of the natural world and of dress.
- The tool also shows the count in each novel: over 43% of the occurrences of scarlet are in a single novel. *Judging from the personal names in the concordance lines (Cipriano, Ramón, Kate) and the descriptions of feathered ornaments and American gods, this novel should be *The Plumed Serpent*, set in Mexico. This is an inference from the concordance lines. The distribution itself is an important reminder: the "author-level" significance of a keyword may come mainly from the subject matter of a single work.*

**Example: colour contrasts in modernist literature.** All 328 texts of the modernist corpus were put in one folder, and syntactic frames were used to search how six colours (red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple) are contrasted. A contrastive structure necessarily contains a lexical trigger or syntactic frame, which makes searching possible.

| Frame type | Trigger | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| explicit opposition | oppose, contrast, difference between, set against; main frame X against Y | Lawrence, *The White Peacock*: the smoke from a cottage rises blue against the trees and thick yellow against the sky; Woolf, *Jacob's Room*: the hills are green against the blue; Wilde: a palace looks purple against a pale-green sky; Wharton: mountains turn purple against a fiery sunset |
| comparative contrast | X-er than Y; more X than Y | Orwell, *Burmese Days*: lips painted "redder than blood"; Kipling: an Atlantic swell "bluer than sapphires"; Wilde: roses "redder than rubies"; Woolf: water "more purple than blue" |

- In Wilde's 26 texts, redder than occurs in four sentences in four texts, yellower than once, and no other colour is contrasted in this frame.
- In X against Y, the Y position is often filled by sky, frequently modified by a colour adjective (blue sky, pale-green sky), and often also by natural things such as sunsets or snow. Filling the Y position with a noun phrase can produce a stronger colour contrast.
- Comparative contrasts often take precious stones (rubies, sapphires, emeralds) or blood as the point of reference.

**Conclusion:** The recurring frame X against Y stresses the balance between opposed colour concepts, letting readers see a clear contrast; as a linguistic device it creates layered perspectives and draws attention to the surrounding context. Colour contrasts often involve other colours and the natural world, such as sky, sunset and snow. *Methodologically, what is searched here is not a single word but a syntactic frame: each colour is substituted in turn into the X position of the frame. This takes corpus stylistics from vocabulary to grammar, and connects it with the analysis of grammatical patterns in P24.*

**Condition: starting from critical insight.** McClure's analysis builds on earlier observations in literary criticism: some critics regard Lawrence as the most important of the modernist writers who saw modernity as deeply damaging to society and the individual. Stylistic analysis (corpus-assisted or not) should not take as its starting point a flat rejection of literary-critical readings of the same text or writer; it should first reflect on the questions critics raise, and then develop an evidence-based description of style, which may support or challenge the criticism.

### Testing Corpus Evidence: Topicality and Generic Provenance

**Problem: who works for whom?** The main challenge of corpus stylistic research is to make the computer work for the analyst, not the other way round. In the early days of corpus linguistics, a speaker presented a large collection of English prose spanning the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, with results showing marked changes in clause patterns over a hundred years. A stylistician in the audience asked: did these results reveal literary motifs and themes common to the two periods? Did the grammatical evidence show writers' understanding of their craft moving from the objective to the subjective? Did subtle changes of style anticipate the Romantic movement? The speaker and the chair replied that the computer had spoken, and the data themselves were the end point of the research.

**Conclusion:** But questions oriented towards stylistics are the only ones worth asking. Corpus stylistic research must strike a balance between quantitative analysis and a broader conceptualization of the relationship between language, style and creativity, which means putting forward hypotheses or research questions about a literary text or a writer's style *before* bringing corpus tools to bear.

**Condition one: topicality.** A database can provide evidence for stylistic analysis only as good as the corpus it rests on. Even with very large corpora, results must be treated with caution. Mahlberg, examining British broadsheets, noticed a marked increase in certain collocates of hand, such as hand gels and hand sanitisers; this reflects the topicality of the news, since these patterns entered the corpus after the 2009 swine flu outbreak. The illness / disease example at the start of this chapter likewise carries the topicality of the Covid pandemic.

**Condition two: generic provenance.** A study of how ordinary language users describe various kinds of `irony` used the British National Corpus to examine the lemma in combination with left-hand adjectival modifiers, such as tragic irony and bitter irony. In raw numbers, the most frequent phrase was heavy irony, with 14 occurrences. But the information before the concordance window is telling:

- all the instances come from written fictional prose;
- the text codes show that all of them come from popular romance fiction;
- four of them come from the same text.

The result has evidently been greatly inflated by its high frequency in one kind of prose fiction. So it is not that heavy is the commonest modifier of irony in the language as a whole; rather, there is evidence that heavy irony is a common, perhaps hackneyed collocation shared and borrowed by authors of one particular *genre* of writing.

**Consequence: evidence opens new questions.** Generic provenance aside, the evidence still raises interesting questions: do the results suggest a gender distinction, with the male hero usually in command of "irony" in these romances? Do heroines tend to be the recipients of irony, or to bear related strategies such as sarcasm and teasing? These are genuine research questions that can be tackled with corpus-assisted analysis.

*This finding has direct implications for genre theory: the "norm" of collocation is itself genre-relative. A combination that looks significant in a general corpus may be merely the formula of one genre. Conversely, an expression ordinary in a general corpus may be a deviation within a particular genre. P40 divides the question "deviation relative to what?" into four kinds of reference point (language, corpus, genre, the text itself), and this is where the corpus reference and the genre reference intersect.*

**Condition three: matching the period.** Setting stylistic analysis beside literary-critical readings of the same text can seek support for the former or propose counter-readings. In *How to Read a Poem*, Terry Eagleton reads Hopkins's "God's Grandeur" (1877) and makes two claims that can be tested with a corpus:

- Starting from the possible monetary sense (charging to an account, levying a fee) of charged in the first line, "The world is charged with the grandeur of God", he sees the same monetary metaphor in spent and dearest, and links them to trade in the first stanza.
- He also suggests that bent in the poem may mean both "literally curved and morally corrupt". The latter sense is embodied in collocations of contemporary colloquial speech such as bent copper (a corrupt police officer).

Would corpus analysis support these readings? One can look up the relevant lemmas in a corpus and narrow the search according to their grammatical environment in the poem. But *Hopkins was a Jesuit priest, and the poem was written in 1877*: using the "corrupt" sense of bent from a corpus of contemporary colloquial speech to support a reading of a nineteenth-century religious poem commits exactly the anachronism described in the first section of this chapter. *Corpora can test claims about connotation, but only if the reference corpus belongs to the right period.*

**Problem: can corpora fail?** The first three sentences of Faulkner's *The Sound and the Fury* are narrated by the mentally disabled Benjy; the third is "Luster was hunting in the grass by the flower tree." Students in classrooms around the world consistently agree that Luster is some kind of animal, which later text shows is not the case. The students' response suggests that something in Faulkner's arrangement of words points to familiar patterns and collocations in the language as a whole. But the corpus does not support this explanation: the commonest left collocates of was hunting and were hunting are human agents.

- One can narrow the search further, including the preposition to the right (was hunting in), or try other combinations.
- If the corpus still cannot satisfactorily explain readers' response, which other stylistic aspects of the sequence, including the co-text of the first two sentences, might shape this impression? *For example: the preceding narration only reports what is seen and never explains ("I could see them hitting"), establishing a perspective of perception without understanding; the name Luster is both uncommon and wholly unintroduced; the action of "hunting in the grass" has no Goal. These belong to the level of mind-style and transitivity (P27), not to the collocation of a single phrase. For Benjy's mind-style, see P42.*
- Perhaps it is simply a puzzle whose solution lies beyond the reach of stylistic analysis.

**Disagreement: do corpora make readers obtuse?** One criticism of corpus-assisted methods holds that they desensitize readers to the subtle, implicit patterns in the fabric of literary texts, patterns that can only really be understood and appreciated through slow, careful, intimate reading. On the other hand, which common sayings and figures of speech really come from Shakespeare, and from which act and scene, can be found in minutes with an online search of the complete works; whether compounds in Joyce's *Ulysses* such as seaspawn, snotgreen and seawrack are hapaxes, and whether they cluster in the "Proteus" episode, can also be quickly established. *The disagreement between the two positions is really about the division of labour: corpora are good at answering "how many, where, and with what", close reading at answering "what does it mean here". All the successful examples in this chapter (Yeats, Dickens, Lawrence) are collaborations between the two, while the Faulkner puzzle shows that neither alone is enough.*

**Tool: a self-check list for corpus stylistic analysis.**

- Before searching, is there already a stylistic question or hypothesis?
- Does the search cover all variants of the lemma? Is the window appropriate?
- Have the concordance lines been filtered by hand (excluding personal names, spurious combinations across clause boundaries, different parts of speech)?
- Do the period, register and genre of the reference corpus match the text analysed?
- Are high-frequency results affected by topicality or by a single source?
- Is the result a tendency or a rule? How are the counter-examples explained?
- After the numbers, has the analysis returned to interpretation: what does this pattern do in this text?

**Transition:** Corpora widen the reference point of stylistics from the single text to the usage of an entire speech community. But the speech community is itself not homogeneous: speakers of different regions, classes and situations use different varieties. How literary texts draw on these varieties to distribute voices is the last question of the foundational part of stylistics (P32).

## P32 How Do Dialect, Register and Style Shifting Shape Voice?

**Background: the sociolinguistic code.** One of the six constituents of narrative discourse (P33) is the `sociolinguistic code`: the total repertoire of language varieties that both derives from and in turn shapes the sociocultural background of the text. It is an organizing resource not only of narrative but of all literary discourse. In monolingual writing this code is largely confined to one language and its sub-varieties; in bilingual writing, several local language varieties are often mixed with a "superordinate" language such as English. Chicano literature from the Mexico–United States border region blends Spanish, English and local Native American forms; in Nigerian literary contexts (as in the work of Soyinka), standard English is mixed with West African Pidgin English and Yoruba. Transitions between languages within a text are called `code-switching`; code-switching in literature marks movement between different fields of reference and has important consequences for thematic intention. Even within a single language, literary works may show marked intralingual variation in their sociolinguistic code, and several key dimensions are set out below.

### Idiolect, Accent, Dialect and Register

**Definition: idiolect.** It is a commonplace of modern linguistics that no two speakers use language in exactly the same way. Everyone has their own linguistic habits and stylistic traits, and the term for an individual's unique style is `idiolect`. *In the novel, idiolect is a character's smallest sociolinguistic unit: a catchphrase or a recurrent syntax is enough to identify a character in dialogue without reporting clauses (P8, P36).*

**Definition: accent and dialect.** Shaped by a speaker's regional origin and socio-economic background, a `dialect` is distinguished by patterns of grammar and vocabulary, an `accent` by patterns of pronunciation. The standard English dialect and the "Received Pronunciation" (RP) accent together make up the high-prestige variety of British English, though in numbers of users they are far outweighed by the many non-standard regional varieties.

|  | Accent (variation in pronunciation) | Dialect (variation in grammar and vocabulary) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| standard | Received Pronunciation (RP) | Standard English |
| non-standard | regional accents (Liverpool, Cockney, Belfast, Glasgow etc.) | regional dialects (Liverpool, Cockney, Belfast, Glasgow etc.) |

**Distinction: Standard English is also a dialect.** It is widely and wrongly believed that Standard English is not a dialect at all, and that together with RP it is "proper" English. One consequence is that critics who talk about "dialect" in literature (in Hardy's novels, for example) often mean only the regional, non-standard, especially rural and conservative dialects used by certain characters. But all speech and writing is framed in some dialect, whether standard or non-standard, high-prestige or low-status.

**Tool: representing accent in writing.** Accent, defined by pronunciation, might seem irrelevant to the stylistic analysis of written literary discourse. But writers have many ingenious means of representing features of speech in print. Irvine Welsh's *Trainspotting* captures the nuances of Edinburgh dialect with a variety of spelling techniques:

- **Vowel lengthening:** a feature of all varieties of Scottish English, shown by doubling vowels, as when got is written goat and off oaff.
- **Monophthongization:** Scottish English retains an older vowel pronunciation going back to Chaucer's time. Most contemporary British accents use a diphthong in words such as about and down, whereas Scottish English uses a long monophthong, spelled aboot and doon.
- **L-vocalization:** the low-status variety of Scottish English that Welsh targets (interestingly, Cockney shares the feature) pronounces /l/ as a vowel rather than a liquid consonant, so ball becomes baw, always eywis and football fitba.

*Deviant spelling here is deviation at the graphological level (P23): it marks sound differences visually and forces readers to read "aloud" in their heads, which is also why such texts lend themselves to reading aloud. But not all non-standard spelling corresponds to a real difference in pronunciation. Spellings such as wuz (was) sound no different from the standard form; they merely label the speaker "non-standard", a practice often called **`eye dialect`**: what it represents is not an accent but a social evaluation of an accent.*

**Definition: hypercorrection and hyperdialectism.** A fictional speaker's attempts to move between accents have marked stylistic appeal for characterization. When shifting from one's own non-standard accent towards a prestige variety, the attempt may misfire and produce `hypercorrection`; misfiring in the opposite direction, from high-status forms towards dialect forms, produces `hyperdialectism`. Over-insertion of /h/ is a common hypercorrection, summed up in a quip: "the 'air of the 'ead but the hair of the hatmosphere", that is, hair and head, which should have an h, lose it, while air and atmosphere, which should not, gain one. Hypercorrection is comic because it suggests the speaker is aspiring to a social status above his actual position; Dickens has a great many such characters.

**Example: "police speak" in *A Brief History of Seven Killings*.** In Marlon James's *A Brief History of Seven Killings* (2014), Nina Burgess, well educated and raised in an affluent district of Kingston, breaks the heel of her shoe during a curfew and is stopped by a group of corrupt and violent police officers. Both sides speak Jamaican Creole (a dialect understood by some 94% of Jamaicans), and Nina also commands Standard English. The dialogue is presented entirely in free direct speech (P8, P36), without reporting clauses, so that readers can tell the speakers apart only by second-person pronouns and alternating forms of address. The police speak `basilectal` Creole: copula deletion (Time not the only thing), simplified inflection and unmarked plurals (one of you foot), and a distinctive interrogative word order (How you was going get home). On top of this naturally "h-less" Creole template is laid a signature h-insertion (h'inna, h'any, h'is), forming a "police speak" used by no other group of characters in the novel. The officers may be trying to produce a standardized, "h-ful" variety befitting authority and official status, but the result is a comically idiosyncratic form. Nina notes this drily in her narration: she wants to point out that none of these words is spelled with an h, but also understands that these men can probably tell when a woman is being rude. *The different fates of the same mechanism in the hands of different speakers are developed in the third section of this chapter and in P47.*

**Definition: register.** Dialect is defined by the users of language and reveals a speaker's social and regional background; `register` is defined by the uses of language: through regular, fixed patterns of vocabulary and grammar, it shows what a speaker or writer is doing with language at the moment. Register is usually described in terms of three features of context: `field`, the setting and purpose of the interaction; `tenor`, the relationship between the participants; and `mode`, the medium of communication, spoken or written.

*The user / use distinction comes from Halliday's theory of register, which belongs, like the transitivity of P27, to systemic functional linguistics: field corresponds roughly to the ideational function, tenor to the interpersonal function, mode to the textual function. Transitivity analyses the realization of field in the clause.*

**Example: copper sulphate.** If the field is set as chemistry, and the language event is specified as written communication between a student and a lecturer, these parameters strongly constrain the type of text expected. Only the first of the two sequences below suits this context:

> (1) A quantity of copper sulphate crystals was dissolved in a beaker containing 200ml of H₂O. The aqueous solution was then heated.

> (2) I was just sayin, Jimmy, that me and my mate Will were putting some copper sulphate stuff into a jug of water the other day. It was bloody great fun.

The vocabulary and grammar of (1) confirm its field as science and its mode as written; the `passive voice`, with no interpersonal markers or forms of address, shows a relatively formal tenor. The first-person pronouns and the evaluative adjective phrase (bloody great) of (2) make it unsuitable for formal scientific prose but suitable for spoken narratives of personal experience (for Labov's model of natural narrative see P34); the `vocative` (the direct address Jimmy) and the swearing further informalize the tenor.

**Distinction: swearing belongs to register, not dialect.** Swearing and taboo language can occur in all social and regional dialects, and are therefore an important feature of register, not, as is commonly supposed, of dialect. *This distinction is crucial in analysis: counting the swearing in *Trainspotting* as "Edinburgh dialect" confuses who the speaker is with what the speaker is doing.*

### Antilanguage and Subculture

**Definition: antilanguage.** An `antilanguage` is a semi-secret language arising in subcultures and alternative societies. These societies, `antisocieties`, are consciously set up as alternatives to mainstream society, their relation to the dominant social order being one of resistance or even active hostility. Antilanguages are therefore typically concerned with illegal drugs, alternative sexual practices or, more generally, the various activities of the criminal underworld (Halliday, 1978).

**Mechanism: relexicalization.** The most important process in forming an antilanguage is `relexicalization`: recycling existing words of the language into new structures and meanings. *Halliday's original account also stresses another process: **`overlexicalization`**, having a great many synonyms for the subculture's central activities (police, theft, drugs). Together the two show that an antilanguage is not just a set of code words but another way of organizing reality: just as an antisociety is an opposition within society rather than outside it, an antilanguage rebuilds a world within language.*

**Example: antilanguage novels.** Antilanguage plays an important part in literary works whose themes are subcultures and antisocieties, often dominating their style completely. Famous examples include William Burroughs's *Naked Lunch* (1959), Hubert Selby Jr's *Last Exit to Brooklyn* (1964) and the model antilanguage novel, Anthony Burgess's *A Clockwork Orange* (1962). *The teenage slang of *A Clockwork Orange*, nadsat, borrows heavily from Russian and anglicizes it, as in droog (friend, from Russian drug) and horrorshow (good, from Russian khorosho). The mismatch in the latter between the English surface (horror show) and the Russian meaning (good) is itself a stylistic effect of relexicalization.*

**Condition: antilanguage did not end with the sixties.** The publication dates of these novels might suggest that antilanguage novels belong to that era alone, but this is not so. Richard Milward's *The Man-Eating Typewriter* (2023) is narrated throughout in Polari (the antilanguage of gay communities), with a great deal of relexicalization (vardaring, feelipalone, meshigena-omi, for instance), so that readers must immerse themselves completely in the text to understand it. The book runs to 534 pages, and some critics and reviewers unfamiliar with Polari called for a dictionary to accompany it.

**Example: the field of drugs in *Trainspotting*.** Welsh's text contains many coded antilanguage references to illegal drugs, various criminal activities, and the police and other authority figures. In the field of "drugs" alone, relexicalization is highly foregrounded: a single page may contain skag, works, smack, gear, speedball, shootin gallery, cookin up and shootin home.

**Consequence: the reader's position.** *Antilanguage places readers in a special position: at first outsiders, they can only infer meanings from context like new recruits (for how inference fills in texts see P39); readers who finish the book have been linguistically "recruited" into the antisociety. This resembles the way genre works: genre calls on unstated knowledge and thereby divides readers into those in the know and those not (P17). Antilanguage is the register that pushes this division to its extreme.*

### The Strategies and Personas of Style Shifting

**Background: there are no single-style speakers.** An axiom of sociolinguistics is that "there are no single-style speakers": everyone can draw on different styles, registers and modes of communication. This strategic capacity in language use is brought to the fore in Marlon James's *A Brief History of Seven Killings*. The novel runs to 686 pages, with 75 characters and more than ten narrators telling events in different styles and codes, presenting multiple internal focalization (P6, P35); these overlapping, alternating interior monologues range from deep Jamaican Creole all the way to American English dialect.

**Definition: the dialect continuum.** Jamaican Creole is itself divided into levels called `lects`, moving step by step away from standard (Jamaican) English. The most esteemed end on the island is the `acrolect`, standard Jamaican English; the farthest end is the `basilect`, the "deepest" Creole. *The transitional levels between the two ends are usually called the **`mesolect`**. The point of the continuum model is that speakers do not "switch" between two languages but slide along a scale, so style shifting can be gradual, partial, even completed within a single sentence.*

**Definition: style shifting.** `Style shifting` refers to a speaker's movement between different styles or lects. Nina Burgess (who in the course of the novel takes the aliases Kim Clarke, Dorcas Palmer and Millicent Segree), privately schooled and raised in an affluent district of Kingston, can use the acrolect yet on many occasions abandons it for Creole. Her dialogue shows style shifting more often than any other character's, displaying many voices and sharply different `personas`. **Naomi Adam**'s stylistic analysis of five of these shifts shows that they are not an unconscious phenomenon but strategies adopted for particular goals, revealing the character's linguistic talent and linguistic awareness.

**Tool: types of style shifting.**

| Type | Driving factor | Nina's example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| interpersonal (convergence) | moving towards the interlocutor's lect, reducing linguistic distance | answering the police, she switches the pronoun in mid-sentence from I to Creole Me |
| affective | emotion such as shock makes the speaker fall back on her linguistic default | taunted by the police, she blurts out a fully articulated standard English "What?" |
| situational | certain discourse situations are bound to particular varieties | Jamaicans often swear in Creole: its swear words are richer and far removed from "classroom" standard English |
| rhetorical | strengthening a position in argument with lectal markers | arguing with her employer in America, she shifts in mid-sentence into Creole subject–verb non-agreement and the pronoun me |

**Example: five personas.** Adam gives each of Nina's five shifts a playful alliterative name.

| Persona | Situation | Strategy and function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pitiable Peasant | stopped by a bodyguard at Marley's door, she falsely claims to be carrying his child | uses the language of a poor countrywoman to play up to the stereotype of "female weakness" and win sympathy |
| Dutiful Deferent | stopped by the police during the curfew | converges on the police basilect for self-protection, taking refuge, as it were, in a linguistic "bolt-hole" |
| Sardonic Sister | woken early by a phone call from her sister and asked about Garveyism | uses exaggerated Creole irony (asking whether she has been put on a radio quiz show) to expose the insincerity of a new convert to Rastafarianism |
| Formidable Foreigner | working as a carer in America under an alias, she quarrels with her elderly employer | usually exaggerates an American accent to mask her Jamaican identity, but shifts into Creole in the quarrel to assert strength |
| Candid Compatriot | working as a nurse in a New York hospital under an alias, facing the wife of a gunshot patient who is also a Jamaican expatriate | interpersonal and situational shifts compete, and her speech rises and falls between lects |

**Mechanism: exploiting stereotypes to expose them.** These motivated shifts are possible because the society of the novel is structurally unequal along axes of gender, class and culture; Nina exposes these stereotypes by linguistically playing up to them. At Marley's door, society's view of women as weaker and more vulnerable actually works in her favour; facing the police, she refers to herself in her inner metalinguistic commentary as "a woman", showing that she knows full well her vulnerability as a lone woman facing several male officers. The first three personas appear in Jamaica, the last two in America; against the American background, "Jamaicanness" stands out more sharply, and the relationship between language and national identity comes to the fore. Creole is versatile in use, and its use and interpretation depend on context: where it is spoken, and by whom it is heard. *The same language is a disguise of the weak in the first two personas and a weapon of the strong in the fourth.*

**Distinction: misfire and mastery.** *The police hypercorrection and Nina's style shifting are two outcomes of the same mechanism: both move towards a perceived target variety. The difference lies in command of the target. The police aim at an "h-ful" standard that exists only in their imagination, and produce forms found in no variety at all; Nina has native-like competence at both ends of the continuum, so her movements hit the mark precisely. The former produces comedy, the latter character: what readers infer from it is linguistic competence, social awareness and calculation for survival (for the indirect presentation of character traits see P5; for characters taking shape in grammar see P37).*

**Distinction: the author's alliances and the character's.** One researcher has suggested that dialect can be used to "build alliances between characters in the fictional world". But in Nina's case, it is less the author than the character herself who builds alliances. *This distinction matters for narratology: style shifting here is not merely the author's means of characterizing but a speech act of the represented character herself; the author's choice is to let the character have choices. For this superimposition of communicative levels see P38.*

**Example: a reverse shift in *Trainspotting*.** Style shifting is also a common source of humour. In the courtroom scene of *Trainspotting*, Renton, charged with stealing books, is asked by the magistrate about Kierkegaard; he suddenly switches to the register of academic philosophy, talking fluently about subjectivity, truth and choice, then stops short, reminding himself inwardly to appear deferential lest being "too clever" bring a heavier sentence. This round trip from Edinburgh dialect to academic English and back is examined in P47.

**Consequence: style shifting by public figures.** Through style shifting people project different images of themselves to the outside world, which matters especially for public figures. Rihanna, born in Barbados and speaking both English and the Creole Bajan, sings most of her work in standard (American) English, but several well-known songs incorporate Creole to varying degrees. On the release of one of them, "Work" (2016), its "unintelligibility" was widely discussed on social media, and some music critics called its lyrics "gibberish". *What such reactions reveal is not so much the unintelligibility of the lyrics as **`language ideology`**: which variety is taken by default to be "intelligible" is itself a distribution of social prestige.*

### The Polyphony of Social Voices in Narrative

**Definition: matrix and satellite varieties.** The "default" pattern in studies of dialect variation in literature is that a standard variety is used for the core narration and description, while regional non-standard varieties are assigned to individual characters. The standard dialect thus forms the `matrix variety` and the non-standard dialects the `satellite varieties`.

**Example: *Trainspotting* inverts the default.** *Welsh's first-person narration is itself written in Edinburgh dialect, which becomes the matrix variety; Standard English is relegated to the satellite position, appearing mainly in the magistrate's questions and in Renton's philosophical monologue. The inversion means that in the discursive order of this novel the "normal" voice is dialect, and it is the official voice that is the marked other. For a layered analysis see P47.*

**Tool: a table for analysing the sociolinguistic code.** Literary discourse can stack or absorb other language varieties, and the difficulty is how to separate these elements rigorously in analysis. The table below offers a method: find an `exponent`, an instance in the text, for each category, and comment on its stylistic impact, especially on how it advances the plot and shapes characters (particularly a first-person narrator).

| Feature of the sociolinguistic code | Points to check |
| --- | --- |
| accent | prestige standard accent? non-standard accent? |
| dialect | standard? non-standard? |
| field | main field? other complementary or conflicting fields? |
| tenor | main tenor? levels of tenor between other participants? |
| mode | by what means does the written medium capture the nuances of spoken dialect? |
| antilanguage vocabulary | which fields are relexicalized? |
| idiolect | which are "personal" features of speech? |

In using the table, remember that swearing and taboo language are variables of register, not of dialect. The table can be adapted to the sociolinguistic codes of other writing contexts; it can be extended to literary code-switching across different languages; and it applies equally to poetry, drama and prose fiction.

**Mechanism: polyphony and complex speech genres.** Rigorously identifying the various styles used by a literary text can illustrate in practice the concept of `polyphony`. **Mikhail Bakhtin** used the term for the "multivoicedness" displayed by certain discourse genres. These genres, called `complex speech genres`, arise in "more complex and comparatively highly developed and organized cultural communication"; in the course of their formation they "absorb and digest" various primary (simple) genres that took shape in unmediated speech communion. Literary discourse is a prominent example of a complex speech genre, with the principle of polyphony at its core. Whatever the academic literary establishment may think of Welsh's work, the analytical table above does show his ability to build a text from multiple and diverse languages and styles.

**Distinction: one mechanism, three descriptions.** *Bakhtin's formulation ties three threads together. In genre theory it is what P15 calls one genre absorbing another: the novel takes in courtroom question-and-answer, philosophical lecture and street slang as primary genres. In narratology it corresponds to the "who speaks?" of P7: a single narrator's voice can contain many social voices, and these voices do not correspond one-to-one with narrative levels. In stylistics it is what the table above sets out to operationalize: polyphony is not an impression but a distribution of varieties that can be identified item by item. For a systematic discussion of Bakhtin's theory of polyphony itself, see P41.*

**Example: *Milkman*, which resists dialect.** Anna Burns's *Milkman* (2018), like *A Brief History of Seven Killings*, won the Booker Prize, and likewise contains intricately layered voices, perspectives and modes of focalization, yet it almost resists non-standard dialect, even where characters and setting would call for it. Set in Belfast at the height of the Troubles, the novel explores fear and repression against a background of violence and intimidation. The creed of the time was not to reveal private feelings, lest one betray one's allegiance, as in the conflict communities' maxim "Whatever you say, say nothing." This goes some way towards explaining the novel's striking stylistic construction: even the first-person narrator is unnamed, referred to only as "middle sister", "longest friend" or "maybe-girlfriend"; places are not named but called "over the water", "over the border", "this side of the road", "that side of the road"; the opposing paramilitary groups are referred to circuitously as "renouncers of the state" and "defenders of the state". Markers of Belfast dialect (such as ach, fellas, ma and da, yer man) are present, but far fewer than a novel set in an urban working-class milieu would be expected to contain.

**Mechanism: reporting without an "original".** This resistance to dialect extends even to speech presentation. Speech presentation assumes the existence of an "original" utterance that can be reported more or less freely or directly (P8, P36); in *Milkman* this assumption plainly fails. When the mother warns her daughter about the dangers of associating with paramilitaries, what follows "according to her" moves into increasingly free direct speech, but it cannot be the mother's actual words, since it is quite unlike the mother's language elsewhere in the novel: it is an almost absurdly antiquated register, full of Latinate vocabulary, multi-unit noun phrases and semantically dense adjective phrases. This very probably stems from middle sister's fondness for eighteenth- and nineteenth-century novels, whose prose style has seeped into her narration. *Here the narrator's voice overrides the voice of the person reported, and the polyphony of social voices is swallowed up by one person's idiolect; yet this swallowing is itself a social voice, the community grammar of "say nothing". See P47.*

**Consequence: metaperspective.** Both Nina in *A Brief History of Seven Killings* and middle sister in *Milkman* are constantly attentive to how others see them, that is, to `metaperspective`: the projection of how others see oneself. Both characters are in some sense socially subordinate (by age, class, ethnicity, gender or religion), which may well be reflected in their overwhelming concern with the gaze of others. *Metaperspective is a type not singled out in the focalization theory of P6 and P35: what the focalizer perceives is not an object but her own image in others' perception.*

**Limitation: the ethical risks of representing dialect.** *Marking non-standard varieties through spelling and grammar always runs the risk of reducing characters to stereotypes. Eye dialect is the extreme form of this danger: it represents no difference of pronunciation, only social evaluation.
