| narratology | an ideological position, a conceptual system for viewing the world | characters' views, behaviour and explicit arguments; the narrator-focalizer's norms | the juxtaposition of Raskolnikov's views with those of other characters in *Crime and Punishment* |
| genre theory | a generically shaped position of enunciation, a compound of manner of speaking and subject matter | genres inserted in the novel, stylized voicing | confessions, diaries, letters, travelogues and biographies absorbed into the novel |

**Mechanism: three kinds of voice linked in one chain.** The three definitions are not rivals but links in one chain: language variety → social identity and position → ideological perspective → generic voice. Stylistics enters at the first link: the sociolinguistic axiom that "there are no single-style speakers" shows that the individual is already multivoiced; genre theory enters at the fourth link: what Voloshinov calls "little speech genres" tie verbal etiquette and tact to social hierarchy, and the various units of discourse in the novel (authorial discourse, narratorial discourse, inserted genres, characters' discourse) each accommodate many social voices; narratology enters at the third link, placing voice in the ideological facet of focalization. One sentence of genre theory closes the chain: "voice", the position of enunciation, is precisely the way generic form becomes recognizable in the novel.

**Example: a clash of registers in court.** The courtroom scene in Welsh's *Trainspotting* (P47) can be read on all three links at once. At the level of language variety, Standard English and Edinburgh dialect coexist; at the level of social position and ideology, magistrate and defendant represent two sets of values that do not recognize each other; at the level of genre, courtroom question-and-answer is a primary genre absorbed into the novel, its built-in structure of power preserved yet presented to readers as performance.

**Disagreement: multivoicedness is not polyphony.** The analytical table of stylistics proves multivoicedness: which varieties a text contains, and where it switches. Narratology's ideological analysis reminds us, however, that a text can be linguistically highly diverse yet ideologically single: so long as all the dialects are evaluated by one dominant narrator-focalizer, these voices are objects on display, not equal subjects. Conversely, a text uniform in syntax and vocabulary can achieve ideological polyphony through characters' views refuting one another. Linguistic diversity and ideological openness are two variables, often found together but not necessarily so.

**Limitation: dialect in literature is stylized.** *Social voices in the novel are not recordings in the sociolinguistic sense but selected, compressed markers: a few features of spelling and vocabulary are enough to signal a dialect. This is exactly what Bakhtin calls "the image of another's language": the novel represents an image of a language, not the language itself.*

**Conclusion:** "Social voice" is, in the three fields respectively, variety, position and generic position. Linking them, one can push from a single spelling feature all the way to the ideological structure of a text; separating them, one can see the gulf between multivoicedness and polyphony.

### Intertextuality, Remakes and Rereading

**Recap:** Intertextuality means that a text is made in relation to other texts; a remake crystallizes the structure of a genre in a single text (P15).

**Problem:** The previous three sections discussed how a text is open to other voices at a given moment. A text is also open in two further directions: towards versions in other media, and towards future readings.

| Direction of openness | Narratology | Genre theory | Stylistics |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| towards other texts | inter-textual polyphony: preserved register makes discourse point to earlier discourse | the text as trace and tracing of others, shaped by repetition and transformation of other texts | intertextuality as a narrative constituent: implicit and explicit allusion |
| towards other media | story can be abstracted from the text and transferred between media and languages (P1) | a remake both takes fragments of its predecessor and displays the historical distance between them | multimodal analysis of adaptation: why films reorder events and cut plot elements (P33) |
| towards future readings | rereading changes how primacy effects, suspense and surprise work (P9) | change of function: later texts rewrite earlier ones (P40) | schema refreshment changes what is foregrounded (P39) |

**Mechanism: remakes and adaptations as experiments on the story / text distinction.** Narratology defines story as what is abstracted from the particular style, language of writing and medium of a text, and so as transferable between media. Adaptations and remakes are natural experiments on this definition: which parts of the story remain unchanged, and which parts of the text change. The multimodal analysis of stylistics asks exactly narratology's question: why is order rearranged, which plot elements are omitted? The film of *Richard III* splits the soliloquy into three places and changes the addressee through shifts in the camera's line of sight (P33). Genre theory adds another layer: what is remade is often not a single predecessor but a whole genre. Herzog's *Nosferatu* follows Murnau's closely, but most of its meaning can be understood even without having seen Murnau's film, because the predecessor belongs to a genre: the pre-text is never single, and never a pure origin.

**Mechanism: two senses of rereading.** Narratology's rereading is the same reader's second reading: the ending is known, primacy effects, suspense and surprise all work differently, and retrospective patterning goes on from the start. Genre theory's rereading is the rereading of one literary system by another: *Crime and Punishment* rewrites *David Copperfield*, *The Trial* rewrites *Bleak House*, and the earlier works thereby become something else. The first kind of rereading changes the dynamics of reading, the second the function of texts. What they share is that later information, an ending or a later text, turns back and changes earlier meanings. This is the counterpart, on the scale of literary history, of the retrospective patterning of P39. A remake is also an open rereading: *A Chorus Line* remakes *42nd Street*, taking the episode in which the star sprains her ankle and a newcomer gets her chance, while letting us see that this is the world of the 1980s rather than the 1930s.

**Disagreement: is intertextuality a device, or a text's mode of being?** Stylistics lists intertextuality as the sixth constituent of narrative, specifically the technique of "allusion", and notes that it partly overlaps with the sociolinguistic code: the former brings in external texts, the latter is the language variety through which a narrative unfolds. Genre theory sees intertextuality as a constitutive condition of texts: no text is unique, otherwise people could neither recognize it nor know how to use it; every text resembles some texts in relevant ways and differs from others in relevant ways, and even "significantly not mentioning" a text is an intertextual relation. Narratology stands in between: it attributes inter-textual polyphony to Bakhtin's description of the novelistic tradition, while acknowledging Derrida's universalization. This is the same disagreement as the strong and weak senses of "citation" in the previous section: in the weak sense, intertextuality is a device that can be identified and can be absent; in the strong sense, it is a condition that cannot be absent.

**Problem: if texts are not closed, how is analysis possible?** Each of the three fields has a means of stabilization. Genre theory says that the relation between text and genre is unstable, but at any given moment "temporarily stable" (P13); narratology confines its objects of analysis to constructs inferred from the text: the implied author, the implied reader, the abstracted story; stylistics requires analysis to be rigorous, retrievable and replicable, that is, to write out openly the frames and reference points used (P22). The three responses to openness are in fact the same: not pretending that the text is closed, but declaring within which frame, with which reference point, and at which moment the analysis is carried out.

**Conclusion:** A text is not closed along three axes: internally it contains several voices (polyphony and social voices), externally it cites and responds to other texts (citation and intertextuality), and in time it is remade, reread and moved into new systems (remakes and change of function). The three fields agree more strongly on this point than on any other cross-topic; they differ only over the strength of openness, and over whether openness abolishes final authority. The synthetic practice chapters that follow apply the tools organized in this part to the texts of a single writer at once.

## P42 Faulkner: Time, Perspective and Mind

Faulkner is one of the writers narratology cites most often, his texts supplying standard instances of order, frequency, focalization, narrative levels and reliability; stylistics in turn uses the opening of *The Sound and the Fury* as a touchstone for mind-style and corpus analysis. This chapter gathers the Faulkner cases scattered across earlier chapters, brings several sets of tools to bear on the same text at once, and marks the level on which each judgement rests.

### "A Rose for Emily": Order, Townspeople's Focalization and Retrospective Reconstruction

**Plot:** Miss Emily Grierson, an old spinster in a Southern town, dies, and the whole town goes to her funeral. The story then moves back and forth across several decades: after her father's death she refuses for three days to give up the body; she keeps company with the Northern foreman Homer Barron and buys arsenic; Homer disappears; a stench comes from her house; she refuses to pay taxes. After the funeral, the townspeople break open an upstairs room that has been shut for forty years: on the bed lie Homer's remains, and on the pillow beside them is a long strand of iron-grey hair.

**Story level / text level: order and frequency.** Abstracted in chronological order, the story begins with the father's death and ends with Emily's death and the opening of the room; the text, however, begins with the funeral and scatters earlier events through it as a series of analepses (P4). In frequency, this story also supplies a case missing from Genette's typology: Emily and Homer's public drives in a yellow-wheeled buggy are said to have taken place every Sunday for about two years, yet the text narrates them four times. This is "narrating several times an event that happened several times, but a different number of times", a kind for which Genette himself said in a footnote he could find no example.

**Level of narration / focalization: one "person", two temporal positions.** Narrator and focalizer are the same "person", a townsman, but they stand in different temporal positions relative to the events narrated. The narrator is temporally external to the story and knows the ending when he begins; yet he chooses not to reveal his retrospective understanding, limiting perception to what the townspeople perceived at the time. The focalizer is therefore not the townsman as narrator, but a group of limited observers at an earlier stage, himself among them (P6). Internal focalization also explains a spatial detail: the interior of Emily's house is described only twice, once when the tax delegation enters and once after her death. For years no one was allowed into the house, and the internal focalizers can see inside only by "accompanying" those who break in. *The recurrent "we" of the narration is the grammatical marker of this arrangement: a collective first person that places the narrator inside the story without granting him a privileged individual view.*

**Level of narration / reading: why the self-restriction?** An external narrator-focalizer is in principle omniscient, and restricting his knowledge is a rhetorical choice: here, to produce surprise and shock. The choice of internal focalizers makes the withholding of information plausible, motivating a retardation by a model of reality (P39). The gap of the smell is thereby established: townspeople and readers alike put it down to a dead rat or snake, and only at the end connect it with the corpse that has lain upstairs for forty years. This is what narratology calls repatterning rather than additional patterning: it does not develop the old meaning further but overturns it, carrying with it a wholesale regrouping of a series of details such as the arsenic, Homer's disappearance and the locked door (P9, P39).

**Story level / text level: how character is inferred.** Emily is an example narratology uses again and again to explain the construction of character, and several mechanisms operate on her at once (P3, P5):

- **Repetition:** the repeated Sunday drives suggest her contempt for the townspeople and her obstinacy.
- **Similarity:** refusing to acknowledge her father's death and preserving her old lover's corpse lead to a generalization: she clings to those who robbed her of her life (the townspeople's interpretation), or her necrophiliac tendencies.
- **Habitual omission:** she repeatedly fails to pay her municipal taxes.
- **Environment:** the dilapidated house, dusty and damp-smelling, is a metonymy of her decline, and its decay is in turn a result of her poverty and morbid temperament.

**Agreement and conflict: three readings of one house.** Narratology explains the decay of the same house in three different places, falling exactly on three levels:

| Reading | Relation it rests on | Level |
| --- | --- | --- |
| metonymy: the house is contiguous with her and caused by her poverty and temperament | contiguity plus causality | story level |
| analogy: the decay of the house parallels her decline | purely textual parallel, independent of story causality | text level |
| literary model: the house is described as decaying to evoke the decline of the South | illustration of theme | level of the naturalizing frame |

The three readings do not exclude one another. Narratology itself grants that metonymy and analogy often overlap in practice, while insisting they are separable in principle: metonymy implies story causality, analogy does not. The force of this detail comes precisely from the layering of three levels: in the story it has a cause, in the text it has a counterpart, in interpretation it has a theme. Using only one tool, it would be merely setting, merely symbol, or merely excerpt.

**Generic level: which frame arrives first.** *From the standpoint of genre theory and the time of inference (P39), the narrative tone of the first half of the story is close to small-town chronicle gossip, activating a frame of manners and rumour; within that frame, arsenic and the smell can be taken as trivia of an eccentric character. The final discovery pushes the text into the frame of the Gothic, and details previously absorbed by the frame of gossip turn into clues. The repatterning therefore takes place both at the level of hypotheses and at the level of generic judgement.*

### "Barn Burning": Prolepsis and the Accumulation of Motive

**Plot:** Ten-year-old Sarty Snopes follows his tenant-farmer father from place to place; whenever his father falls out with a landlord, he burns the landlord's barn. The story opens with a hearing before a justice of the peace at which the boy is called to testify; at the end, the father is again about to burn a new landlord's barn, the boy runs to give warning, hears gunshots, and at dawn walks away without looking back.

**Focalization: the child's present.** The boy is an internal character-focalizer (P6). Internal focalization is synchronous with the information it regulates, confined to the character's "present": the boy knows neither his father's past nor his own future.

**Text level / level of narration: two prolepses.** Yet the text contains two external prolepses that go beyond the boy's present (P4). One is heterodiegetic: the father lashes the mules with a raised willow switch, "but without heat", and the narrator says that this same quality would one day make his descendants race the engine before putting a car in motion. The other is homodiegetic: twenty years later, the boy will tell himself that if he had said then that they wanted only truth and justice, his father would have struck him again anyway. These two prolepses can come only from an external narrator-focalizer in command of all the temporal dimensions. The text therefore switches between two temporal positions: the child's synchronous, restricted present, and the narrator's view across time.

**Reading: prolepsis both fills and creates gaps.** The homodiegetic prolepsis tells readers that twenty years later the boy is still alive and still thinking back to this moment. This closes one suspense (will he be destroyed?) but opens another: what happened between this moment and twenty years later? Narratology points out that prolepsis can create gaps by omitting the stages between the first narrative and the announced future (P9). Suspense shifts from "what will happen" to "how will it happen".

**Reading: the additional accumulation of motive.** Each time a possible arson appears, readers go back to earlier events and collect every detail that might explain the father's motive. This is what narratology calls additional patterning: earlier meanings are not overturned but further exploited and developed. Set against "A Rose for Emily", the two stories demonstrate exactly the two forms of retrospective patterning. In the terms of cognitive stylistics (P39), readers of "Barn Burning" keep extending a schema about the father, while readers of "A Rose for Emily" are forced at the end to dismantle and rebuild a schema about Emily.

**Linguistic level: the narrator's negations.** *This level can be extended with the tools of stylistics. The narrator's description of the father's whipping uses a string of negations: not out of anger, not even sadistic. Among Labov's evaluative devices, negation and "comparison with unrealized events" are precisely forms of evaluation (P34). By ruling out two common explanations (momentary anger, a brutal character), the narrator defines the father's violence as a colder, impersonal "quality", and the heterodiegetic prolepsis that follows extends this quality to his descendants. Negation at the linguistic level and prolepsis at the text level work together here: the former abstracts a trait, the latter generalizes it into a family type.*

**Generic level: the embedded court.** *The story opens with a hearing at which the child is called to testify; the "truth and justice" of the homodiegetic prolepsis is precisely the vocabulary of the courtroom genre. From genre theory's view of embedding (P15), the primary genre of courtroom testimony keeps its structure (a witness must tell the truth), but in the story it is set against a child's loyalty to his family. The boy's final run to give warning can be read as his at last fulfilling, outside the court, what that genre demands of a witness.*

**Agreement and conflict:** In focalization, the label of internal focalization and the presence of external prolepses form an apparent conflict. The solution is to see focalization as locally switchable: overall focalized by the child, shifting briefly to the narrator-focalizer at the prolepses. Narratology's temporal analysis (the prolepses are external) here in turn becomes evidence for the judgement about focalization, an instance of two analytical axes checking each other.

### *The Sound and the Fury*: Benjy's Mind-Style and Jason's Speech

**Plot:** The novel tells of the decline of the Southern Compson family in four parts; the first three are narrated in the first person by three brothers, Benjy, Quentin and Jason, and the fourth switches to the third person. Benjy is a thirty-three-year-old man with severe cognitive limitations, looked after by the Black youth Luster; the novel opens with him watching people play golf through a fence. *The golf course was once the pasture the Compsons sold.*

**Focalization / level of narration: multiple focalization and two kinds of unreliability.** For the novel as a whole, focalization shifts among several characters, a standard example of what narratology calls "multiple focalization" (P6). The different narrators also embody different sources of unreliability (P7, P38): Benjy is an example of limited knowledge, while Jason points to a problematic value system. The novel thus lays out the typology of unreliable narration as a sequence.

**Linguistic level: Benjy's mind-style.** The opening paragraph concentrates the linguistic indicators of a restricted mind (P35). "Golf", "ball" and "club", which readers would use in describing the same scene themselves, do not appear once; in their place are:

- transitive verbs with no Goal element: they were "hitting", without saying what (P27);
- circumlocutory reference through noun phrases: flower tree, curling flower spaces, instead of the names of things;
- strings of coordinate clauses like beads: one and after another, with temporal succession but no causality;
- pronouns of unclear reference: they, he, the other.

**Linguistic level / focalization: what is restricted is categories, not perception.** *Setting these indicators beside narratology's judgement shows exactly where "limited knowledge" is limited. Benjy's reports of perception are not wrong: they really do take out the flag, hit, put the flag back and go to the tee. What he lacks is the category that would put these actions under the script of "golf", and the causality that would connect them. By narratology's classification he is an unreliable narrator; by stylistic analysis he is an extremely precise recorder. The two judgements do not conflict; they show that "unreliable" here means unreliable in interpretation, not in report. In the terms of P39: what Benjy lacks is schemas, not senses.*

**Linguistic level / reading: the second channel.** Restriction can be read as restriction only against a point of reference. The second channel is first supplied by reported speech: Luster's complaints reveal that Benjy is thirty-three, that someone has gone to town to buy a cake, that Luster is looking for a coin so he can go to the show, and the dialect features in them locate the scene in a particular time and place (P35). This in itself refutes the impression of "an idiot's uninformative babble": the passage as a whole provides far more information than it first seems to, only not in Benjy's own words.

**Reading: the reader's own primacy hypothesis.** The third sentence, "Luster was hunting in the grass by the flower tree", leads students in classrooms around the world consistently to take Luster for some kind of animal, though the corpus does not support this association: the commonest left collocates of was hunting are human agents (P31). In the context of this chapter the puzzle gets a fuller description: a primacy hypothesis formed within a restricted perspective (P39). The first two sentences have already established a perspective that only reports what is seen, never names and never explains; the name Luster has no introduction; the action of "hunting in the grass" has no Goal. *A reversal follows: in this sentence it is not Benjy who misunderstands the world but the reader. Benjy knows who Luster is; the reader misreads his own lack of information as the character's restriction. The restricted perspective is not only presented but passed on to the reader.*

**Text level / reading: a retrospective gap.** *In the second paragraph someone calls "Here, caddie", and then Luster tells Benjy to stop moaning. First-time readers do not ask why Benjy is moaning until later text reveals that Benjy's sister is called Caddy, and that she has left home: caddie and the sister's name sound the same. This is a retrospective gap in the narratological sense: readers do not know what they lack until the answer is given (P9). Its form is a pun at the phonetic level, but the pun holds only for readers; for Benjy it is direct: what he hears is his sister's name.*

**Story level / text level: the collapse of time.** *Benjy's section leaps repeatedly between different years, the leaps often triggered by a sensory impression, with a change of typeface often the only marker. In narratological terms these are analepses motivated by a character (P4); but unlike the character's memories in "Eveline", Benjy does not "remember": for him past and present are present at once, and the "present act of recollection" this structure assumes does not exist. In the terms of Text World Theory, this is a string of world-switches without tense markers (P39): sub-worlds are usually marked by tense and deictic features, but here only typeface and content remain as cues. Both sets of terms can describe the phenomenon, but both need an adjustment.*

**Linguistic level / character: Jason's speech.** Jason's section offers another kind of characterization: traits revealed through the content and form of speech (P5). He says he treats everyone the same, regardless of religion, and has nothing against Jews as individuals, "It's just the race." It is mainly the content that reveals his bigotry; but narratology points to two further factors: first, internal contradiction (treating people fairly "regardless of religion" while detesting the Jews as a race), and second, the underlying cliché (the "some of my best friends are Jews" kind of formula), which together highlight the specious logic peculiar to his (and all) bigotry.

**Agreement and conflict: the cliché as citation.** Narratology's analysis of Jason already contains the tools of P41. The "underlying cliché" is a cited social voice: Jason is speaking, but his sentence pattern is a ready-made formula belonging to a certain social group. The implied author lets readers hear this voice and exposes it through internal contradiction; this is one form of double-voiced discourse. *In form, non-standard conjugations such as "I says" also characterize him: the analysis of register and dialect in stylistics (P32) can supply here the "form" half that narratology mentions.*

**Conclusion:** Benjy and Jason give two extremes of narratorial unreliability. Benjy's unreliability lies in categories and causality, shows in transitivity and naming, and requires readers to "see through" it; Jason's lies in values, shows in self-contradiction and cliché, and requires readers to "hear through" it. The former is described most finely by the mind-style of stylistics, the latter by narratology's characterization and genre theory's analysis of citation.

### *Absalom, Absalom!*: Repetitive Narration and Unreliable Testimony

**Plot:** The novel turns on the rise of Thomas Sutpen and the destruction of his family, its central event being the killing by Sutpen's son Henry of his sister's fiancé, Charles Bon. *This history has no omniscient teller; it is retold, guessed at and reconstructed layer by layer, decades later, by Rosa Coldfield, Mr Compson, Quentin and his college roommate Shreve.*

**Text level: thirty-nine times.** Henry's killing of Charles Bon is narrated thirty-nine times, sometimes with changes of narrator, focalizer, duration, narrating agent and style, sometimes without. This is the extreme form of repetitive narration (P4).

**Level of narration: embedding and explanation.** Sutpen tells General Compson about his childhood, especially the humiliation he suffered at the hands of a Black servant; this is a hypo-hypodiegetic level whose function is explicative: it explains how Sutpen lost his innocence and became the self-assertive, amoral man he is (P7, P38).

**Level of narration: Rosa's testimony.** Rosa gives a detailed account of Sutpen fighting with his Black men in front of the children, then adds that she was not there herself and did not see the two Sutpen faces. She is an adult narrator of sound mind who narrates what she does not know; her hatred of Sutpen also constitutes personal involvement. One narrator combines two sources of unreliability.

**Agreement and conflict: where does "the same event" come from?** *Repetitive narration is defined as "telling n times what happened once", which presupposes that the analyst has already established that the n tellings tell the same thing. But in *Absalom, Absalom!* the event itself is reconstructed from conflicting tellings: what the motive was, what happened, who knew, all keep changing. Narratology's classification of frequency therefore depends on a prior judgement: which tellings belong to the same story event. This does not refute narratology, which defines story precisely as an abstraction reconstructed by readers (P1, P34); but it shows that in this text, counting frequency and reconstructing the story are two sides of the same interpretive act.*

**Agreement and conflict: many voices and adjudication.** *Absalom, Absalom! is a testing ground for the question of P41. In the sense of stylistics it is multivoiced: different narrators have different languages. By narratology's ideological analysis, the question is whether there is a final position from which these tellings can be judged. Rosa's "I was not there" shows that the text supplies cues for judgement, while the inconsistency of the thirty-nine tellings shows that these cues never converge into a final hypothesis. In narratology's classification of the fates of hypotheses (P9), it stands between "multiple meaning" and "ambiguity": some versions can complement one another, others are mutually exclusive.*

**Conclusion: four texts, one thread.** Setting the four texts side by side shows Faulkner doing the same thing again and again on three levels: in time, disrupting the correspondence between story and text (analepsis, prolepsis, repetition); in perspective, handing knowledge to restricted observers (the townspeople, the child, Benjy, the absent Rosa); in language, making this restriction a visible pattern (verbs lacking Goals, clichés, negations). The restrictions on the three levels together hand the work of reconstructing the story to the reader. Narratology explains the structure of this work, stylistics its linguistic evidence, and the theory of inference how it unfolds in time.

## P43 Joyce: Focalization, Consciousness and Voice

Joyce is a key case in all three fields: narratology uses him to distinguish "who sees" from "who speaks", genre theory regards Stephen's aesthetics as one of the clearest summaries of the tradition of the "three natural forms", and stylistics uses *Ulysses* to demonstrate stream of consciousness, text worlds and onomatopoeia. The four sections are arranged along one thread: how the narrator borrows the character's language, how a character theorizes the withdrawal of the narrator, how narrator and character share a sentence, and in what form the narrator returns after he seems to have vanished.

### *A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man*: A Child's Perception and the Narrator's Language

**Plot:** The novel follows Stephen Dedalus from early childhood to young manhood, until he resolves to leave Ireland and become an artist. It opens with a story a father tells his small child:

> Once upon a time and a very good time it was there was a moocow coming down along the road and this moocow that was coming down along the road met a nicens little boy named baby tuckoo… / His father told him that story: his father looked at him through a glass: he had a hairy face.

**Level of narration / focalization: who sees, who speaks.** It is generally agreed that almost everything in this novel passes through Stephen's eyes. Booth held that any sustained inside view temporarily turns the character into a narrator; if this is accepted, Stephen is both focalizer and narrator. Narratology uses this opening to refute the confusion (P6). The language conveys the child's perception and includes baby talk; but it is not Stephen's language, and Stephen is not the narrator of this passage. There are two reasons: a baby who still wets the bed (see the next paragraph) could not utter complete sentences like those above; and in this passage Stephen appears in the third person (he, him), which would be an unlikely practice if he were the narrator himself (though one might argue that children often talk this way). The conclusion is that in novels with a "third-person centre of consciousness", the centre of consciousness (the reflector) is the focalizer, and the one using the third person is the narrator.

**Linguistic level: child language that is not free indirect discourse.** What is special about this passage is that baby talk enters the narration but cannot be attributed to the character's speech or thought. Applying the stylistic categories of speech and thought presentation (P36) meets difficulties: free indirect thought presupposes that the character has a thought that can be reported, and a baby has no organized sentences to report. What enters the narration here is the focalizer's perception and lexical colouring: baby-talk forms such as moocow, nicens and baby tuckoo, and details only a child would notice, such as the father's "hairy face". Narratology's theory of focalization is more serviceable here than the categories of speech presentation: it allows the perceiving subject and the speaking subject to come apart without requiring the former to possess a sentence. *The Joyce scholar Hugh Kenner calls this practice, in which narrative language absorbs a character's idiom, "the Uncle Charles Principle".*

**Level of narration / generic level: an embedded story.** The first sentence is in fact the story the father tells, a hypodiegetic narration; it has no quotation marks and no reporting clause, and is located only by the second sentence, "His father told him that story". From the standpoint of genre theory, "Once upon a time" is a formula of the oral tale genre, and the novel opens by citing a primary genre (P15, P41). Three sets of tools overlap on this sentence: in narrative level, it is an unmarked embedded narration; in genre, it is a keyed fairy-tale formula; in focalization, it is the story as the child hears it, not as the father tells it. *The "baby tuckoo" of the story is the listening child himself, and the immediately following "He was baby tuckoo" identifies the character inside the story with the listener outside it: a small transgression of levels, and the starting point of a self-image.*

**Agreement and conflict:** Narratology and stylistics agree that the narrator's language can be coloured by the character; they differ over which categories to use in saying so. The classification of stylistics takes reported speech and thought as its unit, suited to adult characters; narratology's focalization takes perception as its unit, suited to a consciousness not yet able to organize sentences. *The narrative language of the whole novel changes as Stephen grows, from baby talk to schoolboy idiom to aesthetic disputation, which also means that the ranges of application of the two sets of categories shift as the novel proceeds: the further on, the more serviceable the description in terms of free indirect thought.*

### Stephen's Aesthetics and the "Three Natural Forms"

**Plot:** In chapter five of the *Portrait*, the university student Stephen expounds his aesthetic theory to his fellow student Lynch as they walk. The passage on the three forms of art reads:

> Art necessarily divides itself into three forms progressing from one to the next. These forms are: the lyrical form, the form wherein the artist presents his image in immediate relation to himself; the epical form wherein he presents his image in mediate relation to himself and to others; the dramatic form, the form wherein he presents his image in immediate relation to others.

He goes on to say that in the dramatic form the personality of the artist is at first a cry, a cadence or a mood, then a fluid and lambent narrative, and finally refines itself out of existence, impersonalizes itself, so to speak.

**Generic level: the summary of a tradition and its doubtful points.** Genre theory regards this passage as one of the clearest summaries of the whole tradition that treats the three "natural" forms as having essential properties (P16). "Progressing from one to the next" is both a theory of psychological stages and a theory of historical development, the one mapped onto the other. But taking the "immediate" or "mediate" relation between self and others as the criterion produces ambiguities in each of the forms:

- What exactly is drama's "immediate relation to others"? There are really two kinds of others here: the others of epic are fictionally represented, whereas the others of drama are embodied, self-representing sources of speech.
- Does putting self and others on the same plane blur important distinctions between author, position of enunciation and fictional character?
- In what sense is lyric an "immediate relation" to the self? Can the "I" of the lyric not be seen as a kind of character, a shaped image, rather than a direct expression of the self?
- And how would the difference between first-person and third-person narration affect the "mediate relation" between artist and characters?

**Level of narration: narratology's answer.** The last two questions raised by genre theory can be answered exactly by narratology's categories.

- **Author, position of enunciation and character:** narratology separates real author, implied author and narrator (P7). The artist Stephen describes as "refined out of existence" is close, in narratological terms, to the implied author: it has no voice in any case, instructing readers silently only through the design of the whole. But narratology also holds that the narrator is a constitutive, not an optional, factor in narrative communication; even the most covert narration has a narrator. Understood as "without a narrator", Stephen's "dramatic" ideal is exactly the "narratorless narrative" narratology opposes.
- **First person and third person:** one of narratology's conclusions is precisely that, as far as focalization is concerned, there is no difference between a third-person centre of consciousness and first-person retrospective narration: in both the focalizer is a character in the represented world; the only difference is who the narrator is. Stephen treats "mediate relation" as a single scale; narratology splits it into two independent variables: who sees, and who speaks.

**Level of narration / generic level: who proposes this theory.** This aesthetics is spoken by a character in dialogue. By narratology's analysis of the ideological facet of focalization (P6), a character's ideology is not necessarily the norm of the text; by genre theory (P15), this is a genre absorbed into the novel, the philosophical dialogue or lecture, which keeps the structure of theory in the novel but has its theoretical authority suspended, becoming material for characterization. *Whether Stephen's theory should be taken as Joyce's aesthetic programme or as a young man's self-fashioning is a long-standing debate in the history of criticism; the three sets of tools cannot settle it themselves, only show that it depends on how readers judge the distance between the implied author and this character.*

**Agreement and conflict: three identities of one passage.** The same passage has three identities in the three fields: genre theory treats it as a theoretical proposition and tests whether its criteria of classification are consistent; narratology treats it as a character's discourse and locates it in narrative communication; stylistics can treat it as a stretch of language and attend to its own form: three parallel appositives, a set of opposed terms built from immediate and mediate, and the persuasive force, independent of content, that this parallel structure itself brings. *Genre theory quotes Genette to the effect that the triad is a "too seductive" pattern; from the standpoint of stylistics, what seduces is precisely its parallel form, the poetic function at work in theoretical discourse (P26).*

### "Eveline" and "Araby": Anachrony and Double Focalization

**Plot:** In "Eveline", a young Dublin woman sits at a window, preparing to elope with the sailor Frank to Buenos Aires, recalling the past and imagining the future; at the quay she grips the railing and does not board. In "Araby", a boy infatuated with his friend's sister promises to bring her a present from the "Araby" bazaar; delayed by his uncle's late return, he arrives as the bazaar is closing, and in the darkness sees his own vanity. Both stories are from *Dubliners* (1914).

**Text level: Eveline's anachronies.**

> But in her new home, in a distant unknown country, it would not be like that. Then she would be married—she, Eveline. People would treat her with respect then.

The prolepsis here, and the analepsis earlier in the story (the field where she once played with other children), cannot be attributed directly to the narrator; they are filtered through the character's memories, fears and hopes, motivated by the character. They do not wholly depart from chronology: the acts of remembering and hoping are themselves part of the linear unfolding of the first narrative, and only their contents belong to the past or the future. In abstracting the story, these events would probably appear twice (P4).

**Linguistic level: the same sentence is free indirect thought.** The sentence quoted above has the typical features of free indirect thought (P36): third person and backshifted tense (would), no reporting clause, yet the character's emotional stress is kept within the sentence. The appositive repetition "she, Eveline" belongs to her own self-affirmation, not to a detached narrator. Narratology's "anachrony motivated by a character" and stylistics' "free indirect thought" describe two sides of the same fact here: the former says what happens in time, the latter how it is done in grammar.

**Focalization / character: the window and the dusting.** When an internal focalizer is in a closed room, the room can be presented through her eyes, but the street cannot, unless there is a window she looks out of. Eveline sitting at the window is an example of this spatial restriction (P6). Her habitual dusting of the house is what narratology calls a habitual action: habitual actions tend to reveal a character's constant, static side (P5). The gaze from the window and the repeated dusting point on two levels to the same ending: spatially she can see only the street, as a character she is someone who does not change.

**Linguistic level: the "subconscious" in the corpus.** A corpus stylistic study found in "Eveline" several subtle "subconscious hints" that, contrary to the explicit signals of the plot, suggest she will not leave home in the end. Another study applied Propp's functions to a passage of this story (P34).

**Agreement and conflict: plot signals and lexical patterns.** *The two analyses give prospects pointing in opposite directions: at the level of story, leaving is the announced action; at the level of language, staying is the prepared ending. The refusal at the quay can therefore be read in two ways: for readers following only the plot, it is a repatterning, overturning the hypothesis of elopement; for readers who have noticed the lexical hints, it is only an additional patterning, confirming a pattern already present (P39). What the corpus does is reveal on a first reading what most readers feel only in retrospect.*

**Focalization: the two focalizers of "Araby".** "Araby" is an adult narrator telling of his childhood self. His language is sometimes coloured by his perception at the time of narration (external focalization), sometimes by the perception of his younger self (internal focalization), and sometimes ambiguous between the two (P6). The various markers can be set out in a table:

| Marker | Example | Points to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| evaluative adjectives | her name was like a summons to all my foolish blood | adult narrator |
| temporal and cognitive distance | I forgot whether I answered yes or no: "forgetting" can only be known afterwards | adult narrator |
| a child's associations | likening the silence of the empty bazaar to a church after a service | child |
| emotional, illogical causality | I liked the last best because its leaves were yellow | child |
| ambiguity | I imagined that I bore my chalice safely through a throng of foes | as the child's fantasy, the stress falls on the world of religious ritual; as the narrator's view, on the clichéd quality of this imagining, in an ironic tone |

**Linguistic level / focalization: the last sentence.**

> Gazing up into the darkness I saw myself as a creature driven and derided by vanity; and my eyes burned with anguish and anger.

The alliterations driven and derided, anguish and anger plainly belong to the narrator; gazing echoes the opening description of the houses that "gazed at one another", and the child's "blindness" connects with the "blind" street of the opening. But does the self-awareness of "I saw myself" belong to the child at the time or to the adult years later? The sentence offers no definite cue. The phonetic level (alliteration) and the level of lexical cohesion (gazing, blind) both assign the sentence to the narrator, while the self-knowledge at the level of content cannot be assigned. This is exactly the second kind of dual voice in the first person described in P36: between the narrating I and the experiencing I, where neither person nor tense can tell the two apart.

**Generic level: the frame the child uses to understand the world.** *The imagery of "chalice" and "foes" shows that the child places his errand within the frame of chivalric quest and religious ritual, and the name "Araby" evokes Oriental romance. In the terms of P39, this is a character using a generic schema. The self-knowledge at the end is therefore a repatterning taking place within the story: the child himself dismantles the frame of romance and rereads everything before as vanity. The character's repatterning and the reader's happen in the same sentence.*

**Agreement and conflict: two stories, one variable.** One of narratology's conclusions is that, as far as focalization is concerned, there is no difference between a third-person centre of consciousness and first-person retrospective narration; only the narrator differs. The two stories are exactly a controlled comparison of this conclusion: Eveline and the child of "Araby" are both internal focalizers; the difference is who speaks. In "Eveline", the dual voice is between an impersonal narrator and the character, identified by the grammatical markers of free indirect thought; in "Araby", it is between two ages of the same person, identifiable only by the lexical markers of focalization. The grammatical categories of stylistics are most effective in the former case, narratology's markers of focalization in the latter.

### *Ulysses*: Stream of Consciousness, Sub-Worlds and Nonlexical Onomatopoeia

**Plot:** The novel is confined to a single day in Dublin, 16 June 1904. Bloom, an advertising canvasser, attends an acquaintance's funeral in the morning (the "Hades" episode) and in the afternoon listens to singing in a hotel dining room (the "Sirens" episode); another strand follows the young Stephen, walking alone on the strand (the "Proteus" episode); the book ends with the monologue of Bloom's wife, Molly.

**Linguistic level / level of narration: two descriptions of stream of consciousness.** Stylistics analyses stream of consciousness as free direct thought plus grammatical ellipsis (P36); narratology sees free direct discourse as the typical form of first-person interior monologue (P8), takes Molly as the extreme of the axis of "penetration into the inner life" (P3), and also as an example of someone who is both focalizer and focalized (P6). The two descriptions correspond to two dimensions of the same kind of writing: what form it takes grammatically, and in narrative communication who sees and what.

**Text worlds: sub-worlds in "Hades".** After Bloom's conversation with the cemetery caretaker O'Connell, his thoughts run like this:

> You might pick up a young widow here. Men like that. Love among the tombstones. Romeo. Spice of pleasure. In the midst of death we are in life. Both ends meet. Tantalizing for the poor dead. Smell of frilled beefsteaks to the starving gnawing their vitals. Desire to grig people. Molly wanted to do it at the window. Eight children he has anyway.

Text world analysis yields several layers of observation (P29):

- **Deictic anchoring:** the here of the first sentence anchors the thoughts in the text world of the cemetery.
- **Three experiential domains:** sex, death and food continue from one sub-world to the next in a radial structure, and the same word can point to more than one experiential domain at once. One critic says that Bloom's thoughts spread "centrifugally" outwards from the figure of O'Connell; the task of stylistics is to supply linguistic evidence for such critical intuitions.
- **World-switches and binding:** from "Molly wanted to do it at the window" to "Eight children he has anyway", the change of tense pulls readers back from a sub-world of memory to the present. The antecedent of he is not the most recently mentioned "Romeo" but O'Connell several lines earlier: he has never been unbound from the location of the cemetery, and readers must re-prime a character bound in long before.
- **Intertextual sub-worlds:** some projections evoke other texts, especially other literary works, such as Romeo.

**Generic level / citation: an inverted scripture.** *"In the midst of death we are in life" inverts a line from the burial service in the Church of England's Book of Common Prayer: "In the midst of life we are in death".* Seen with the tools of P41, this is a cited formula: the syntactic structure of the scripture is kept, but its two nouns are swapped, the force of the religious ritual suspended, turning it into a playful twist as Bloom thinks of sex and life at a funeral. In Text World Theory it is an intertextual sub-world, in genre theory a keying, in Bakhtin's vocabulary a double-voiced utterance. The three descriptions are of one and the same thing.

**Phonetic level / reading: the end of "Sirens".** The nonlexical onomatopoeia at the end of "Sirens" (P25) can be read here together with the other three sets of tools:

> Nations of the earth. No-one behind. She's passed. Then and not till then. Tram kran kran kran. Good oppor. Coming. Krandlkrankran. I'm sure it's the burgund. Yes. One, two. Let my epitaph be. Kraaaaaa. Written. I have. / Pprrpffrrppffff. / Done.

- **Level of reading:** the episode opens with a string of unintelligible fragments (including Fff! Oo! and Kraa. Kraandl.), which can only be interpreted in retrospect. This is a version, at the phonetic level, of temporary gaps and retrospective patterning in the narratological sense (P9): onomatopoeia carries no meaning of its own, its referent waiting to be fixed by later context. And the hints of breaking wind have been prepared bit by bit over the previous pages, their final release being the climax of a small private drama, an additional accumulation.
- **Level of citation:** what Bloom is looking at are the last words of the Irish patriot Robert Emmet about the Irish nation, which are chopped up and alternate with Bloom's physiological situation. The genre of heroism is cited and deflated: the \[p\] and \[f\] of epitaph, the most prominent word in the last words, echo the fart, exposing the heroic gesture at the very moment it is made. This is the irony and parody of P40: evoking a genre and distancing oneself from it.
- **Level of voice:** wordplay in the episode such as Seabloom, greaseabloom is not Bloom's own thought but a narrative voice playing musically with words. The label of free direct thought does not fully apply here: the narrator has not disappeared; he has come back in the form of the sound of language rather than of commentary.
- **Level of mimesis:** the analysis of nonlexical onomatopoeia shows that its sense of aptness does not come mainly from resemblance between the sounds of language and the sounds of the external world; onomatopoeia is "a convention within convention", and the only truly successful onomatopoeia occurs in imitating the human voice, which is in a sense what written language does all the time. This confirms, on two levels, a claim of narratology: language can imitate only language, and narrative fiction can produce the illusion of mimesis only through narration (P8). Onomatopoeia, like direct speech, is "directness" produced within convention.

**Linguistic level: the corpus and two minds.** A great many words in *Ulysses* are used only once, and these hapaxes cluster in key episodes, such as "Proteus", in which Stephen walks on the strand (P31). *This offers a testable hypothesis: Stephen's mind-style is marked by a high density of coined compounds and learned vocabulary, Bloom's by everyday, practical vocabulary full of commodities and food. Statistics of hapaxes and keywords by episode could turn this intuition into replicable evidence.*

**Generic level: an ironic title.** The title "Ulysses" is not the protagonist's name, but its position as title suggests an analogy with Bloom, and the contrast between mythic hero and modern counterpart casts an ironic light on the latter (P5). *From the logic of the remake in genre theory (P41), the whole novel can be seen as a "remake" of an epic: it takes the structure of the *Odyssey*'s homecoming and the correspondence of episodes, while making visible the historical distance between the two. Narratology's analogy, genre theory's remake and stylistics' style shifting describe here three scales of the same ironic structure: a name, a genre, a set of styles.*

**Agreement and conflict:** Stream of consciousness is often described as the disappearance of the narrator. Taken together, the three sets of tools show that the narrator has not disappeared but changed his manner of presence. Narratology insists in principle that the narrator is a constitutive factor of narrative; stylistics' free direct thought describes the passages where the narrator steps back, but "Sirens" shows him returning in the form of phonetic play; genre theory and Text World Theory show that even in the purest interior monologue the character's thoughts are full of other people's cited words (scripture, Romeo, Emmet's last words). Stream of consciousness is not a single voice but a dialogue between a mind and the countless voices it carries.

**Conclusion: Joyce as a laboratory of "who speaks".** The four sections give four answers to the same question. The opening of the *Portrait*: the narrator speaks, but in the child's words; Stephen's aesthetics: a character speaks, saying that the narrator should disappear; "Eveline" and "Araby": narrator and character share a sentence, across two persons in the former, across two ages of one person in the latter; *Ulysses*: the character's thoughts are presented directly, yet the narrator reappears in the form of sound. Narratology's theory of focalization, stylistics' speech and thought presentation, and genre theory's citation and embedding each have most explanatory power at different positions in this sequence.

## P44 Dickens: Retrospection, Causality and Grammar

Dickens appears in different ways in the three fields: narratology uses *Great Expectations* to discuss retrospective narration, causality and gaps; stylistics uses the opening of *Bleak House* to demonstrate grammatical foregrounding, and a Dickens corpus to test impressions of style; genre theory places Dickens in later literary systems to see how he is reread. This chapter lets these tools meet on a single writer.

### *Great Expectations*: Experiencing Self and Narrating Self

**Plot:** The orphan Pip is brought up by his sister and the blacksmith Joe, and as a small child helps an escaped convict on the marshes; he is summoned to the house of the reclusive Miss Havisham and falls in love with Estella, whom she has raised; later an anonymous benefactor gives him "great expectations", and he goes to London to become a gentleman, until he discovers that his benefactor is the convict Magwitch. The novel is narrated retrospectively by the adult Pip.

**Level of narration: a homodiegetic narrator who knows "everything".** The adult Pip is an extradiegetic, homodiegetic narrator telling his own story (autodiegetic). Though not omniscient in principle, he knows "everything" about the story at the time of narration: who the mysterious benefactor is (though he withholds this key detail from readers for a long time), what is happening simultaneously elsewhere (Estella's marriage and separation while he is in London and Cairo), and the deepest feelings of characters (Miss Havisham's vengeful motive in using Estella to break men's hearts) (P7, P38).

**Focalization / linguistic level: two Pips.**

> 'You are to wait here, you boy,' said Estella; and disappeared and closed the door. I took the opportunity of being alone in the court-yard, to look at my coarse hands and my common boots. My opinion of those accessories was not favourable. They had never troubled me before, but they troubled me now, as vulgar appendages.

This records what the child saw, felt and understood at the time, but words such as accessories and appendages are plainly not in a child's vocabulary. The narrator is the adult Pip, the focalizer the child Pip (P6). More precisely, the facets of focalization belong to different agents: the perceptual focalizer is usually the young, experiencing Pip, while ideology tends to be focalized by the older, narrating Pip; and the narrator Pip also often acts as focalizer, so that the story is focalized sometimes by the experiencing child, sometimes by the adult narrator.

**Linguistic level: first-person free indirect thought.** *In "They had never troubled me before, but they troubled me now", now is used together with the past tense troubled: the proximal temporal deictic belongs to the child's present, tense and vocabulary to the adult narrator. This is a typical marker of free indirect thought, only occurring in the first person: the second kind of dual voice described in P36, in which the narrating I and the experiencing I share a sentence. In one sentence, the lexical level (accessories) and the deictic level (now) point respectively to two different ages.*

**Character: static yet complex.** Narratology uses *Great Expectations* to revise Forster's dichotomy of "flat / round" (P3). Joe and Wemmick are static, yet clearly have more than one quality; Miss Havisham's lack of development is presented as an arrest caused by psychological trauma, which gives complexity to a static character; many of Dickens's flat characters are not only very "alive" but give an impression of depth. Pip himself is a fully developed character, and his development is measured precisely by the distance between the two Pips.

**Agreement and conflict: a comparison with "Araby".** Both works are first-person retrospective narratives, both moving between an adult narrator and a child focalizer (P43). The difference lies in the ideological facet: in *Great Expectations*, evaluation is stably attributed to the adult Pip; in the last sentence of "Araby", the attribution of self-knowledge cannot be determined. *In the vocabulary of P41, *Great Expectations* is closer, as between its two selves, to what Uspensky calls the "simple case": the young Pip's evaluations are contained and adjudicated by the older Pip's, the former turning from subject of evaluation into object of evaluation; but the young Pip's perceptions keep their own vividness, which is the part the narrator cannot take back.*

### The Secret Benefactor: Causality, Gaps and Retrospection

**Story level: two kinds of "why".** Early in the novel, why does the six- or seven-year-old Pip help the convict? Two different answers are possible (P2): by the logic of verisimilitude (which the text itself foregrounds), the child is frightened into submission; by the structural requirements of the plot, the action is indispensable, so that Magwitch will feel grateful to Pip and want to reward him; without it, the plot would not be this plot. The latter is in fact teleological, often understood as "forward causality", as distinct from the "backward causality" of the former.

**Level of narration / reading: a retrospective gap.** The question "who is Pip's secret benefactor?" is not seriously raised before the answer is supplied by the events themselves; only afterwards do readers realize that important information has been withheld. This is what narratology calls a retrospective gap (P9). At the same time, the analysis at the level of narration says that the adult Pip knows who the benefactor is but withholds it from readers for a long time.

**Agreement and conflict: why is the gap not noticed?** *Putting the two judgements together raises a question: the narrator is withholding, so why do readers not ask? The answer lies at the level of focalization. The young Pip himself believes his benefactor to be Miss Havisham, and since the story is mainly focalized by him, this false belief fills the gap in advance as a default. In the classification of P39, this is "disguising a gap as a default", isomorphic with the "dead rat" of "A Rose for Emily" (P42); only here the source of the disguise is a character's belief rather than a group of townspeople's conjecture. The narrator need not lie; he has only to hand perception to the child of the time to withhold the answer legitimately. What narratology calls "an external focalizer restricting his knowledge for rhetorical reasons" is realized in exactly this way in first-person retrospective narration.*

**Reading: the temporal distribution of two kinds of causality in reading.** *The two kinds of causality coexist at the level of story, but appear one after the other in the time of reading. On first reading the scene on the marshes, readers see only the causality of verisimilitude: a frightened child. Only when the benefactor's identity is revealed does the scene acquire its structural meaning: it is the starting point of the whole plot. "Forward causality" becomes visible only in retrospect, a correspondence between narratology's analysis of causality (P2) and the dynamics of reading (P9): teleological causality is a product of repatterning.*

**Generic level: Pip's fairy-tale frame.** *The young Pip's false belief about Miss Havisham can be seen as his using a fairy-tale schema to understand his own life: the eccentric, wealthy old woman is the fairy godmother, and the beautiful girl she has raised is the destined bride. The revelation that the benefactor is a convict replaces this frame with a frame of social reality. As with the child of "Araby", this is a character using a generic schema and finally being forced to give it up (P39, P43). The gap goes unnoticed partly because readers also recognize this fairy-tale schema and accept its defaults along with the character.*

### The Fog of *Bleak House*: Grammatical Foregrounding

**Plot:** *Bleak House* centres on an inheritance suit in the Court of Chancery that has dragged on for generations, and is told alternately by two narrators: an anonymous narrator using the present tense, and the first-person retrospection of the orphan Esther Summerson. The novel opens with the fog over London:

> Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping …

**Linguistic level: five grammatical features.** The stylistic analysis (P24, P26) can be summed up in five points, here matched item by item with narratological categories:

| Grammatical feature | Effect | Narratological counterpart |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the head noun fog takes no modification, whereas the surrounding nouns are modified | the fog seems bare, undifferentiated, undetermined | — |
| the predicate of the main clause is either omitted altogether or reduced to creeping, lying, pinching without a finite element | a sense of process but no tense; space is fully anchored, time cannot be fixed | *a descriptive pause at the opening: a stretch of text corresponding to zero story duration (P4). Tenseless syntax is precisely the linguistic form of the pause* |
| many "trailing" constituents pile up to the right of the predicate; it can refer to the fog or the river | rich detail of place, sparse detail of time; ambiguity of reference reinforces visual vagueness | — |
| spatial focus narrows step by step from "everywhere" to the stem and bowl of a skipper's pipe; transitivity moves from no Goal to the goal-directed cruelly pinching | the further on, the more threatening and malevolent the fog | spatial focalization moving gradually from a bird's-eye panorama to the local (P6); panoramas are common at the openings of narratives |
| the sixth sentence changes Subject, moving fog to the right of the predicate | internal foregrounding: the text violates the norm it has established | — |

**Focalization: "as if they were up in a balloon".** The sixth sentence says that people on the bridges peep over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the misty clouds. *This simile writes narratology's "bird's-eye" perspective into the story itself: after a description that has narrowed step by step from panorama to detail, the text gives characters a high vantage point, and from this vantage point nothing can be seen. The panoramic privilege of the external focalizer is cancelled here by the fog.*

**Level of narration: two narrators and two tenses.** Esther's narration begins with her saying that she finds it hard to begin writing her portion, because she knows she is not clever; she always knew that. This is commentary on the narration, concerned not with the represented world but with the problem of representing it; but her self-deprecation does not shake the fictional reality of the story she tells, unlike the footnotes that overturn the main text in Beckett's *Watt* (P7, P40). *The expression "my portion" itself exposes the division of narrative labour: she knows she is writing only part of the book. The anonymous narrator's tenselessness and present tense, and Esther's past tense, are in Text World Theory two worlds distinguished by tense (P39), and in narratology two narrators and two times of narration (simultaneous and subsequent narration).*

**Generic level: "Dickensian" or headline-like?** Stylistics offers a comparison. A sports website headline, "Everton eyeing shock Moyes return", likewise uses a predicate without a finite element, eyeing. The question is: can this headline be said to have a "Dickensian" flavour? Or does Dickens's writing have the flavour of sports journalism? Does grammatical similarity invite the same interpretation? Genre theory's analysis of headlines points towards the answer: compression, nominalization and the suppression of verb forms are formal features of the genre in news headlines, working together with generic effects such as urgency, recency and "this is true" (P10, P17). The same grammatical pattern means "happening now, and important" in a news headline, but at the opening of a novel "time has stopped, and only space is left". This is another example of "one pattern, opposite verdicts" in P40: with a different reference genre, deviation and norm change places.

**Tool: counter-rewriting.** Stylistics sets against the original a thoroughly "un-foggy" sentence: "Across the Essex Marshes, a thick choking fog of indistinct proportion was sweeping in", a thoroughly "un-Dickensian" sentence. It adds modification to the fog, tense to the predicate, and brings the place to the front of the sentence. Counter-rewriting works because it sets up, temporarily, a norm for comparison (P40).

**Agreement and conflict:** Narratology's "pause" and "panorama" can say what this passage is in terms of story time and spatial location, but not why it reads the way it does; stylistics can say which grammatical choices produce the sense of timelessness and threat, but needs narratology to show what place these choices occupy in the temporal structure of the whole novel; genre theory reminds us that the same choices would have quite different effects in other genres. Together, the three show that the meaning of a grammatical pattern lies not in the pattern itself but in its relation to narrative position and generic frame.

### Dickens in the Corpus and Dickens Reread

**Linguistic level: the evidence of as if.** A corpus study based on 23 works by Dickens and 29 other nineteenth-century texts found that as if in Dickens often collocates with action verbs, body-part nouns and look, describing characters' body language and appearance: external description takes precedence over psychological explanation (P31). This finding grounds earlier impressions of Dickens's "grim grotesque", characterizing from the outside, without psychological explanation, but with intense attention to bodily features; and since the examples come from five different novels, the corpus supplies both micro-detail and a bird's-eye view.

**Focalization: words of estrangement.** The psychological facet of narratology supplies a precise counterpart (P6). The focalized may be perceived from within, often marked by "he thought", "he felt" and the like; or only from without, inner states left to be inferred from outward behaviour, in which case modal expressions often appear that mark the conjectural nature of the inference: "evidently", "apparently", "as if", "seemed", what Uspensky calls `words of estrangement`. *The Dickensian as if discovered by the corpus is precisely the statistical distribution of words of estrangement across a writer's entire output. Narratology supplies the category, the corpus the frequency; the former shows what the word does in narration (keeping the inner life outside, conjecturing rather than asserting), the latter that this is Dickens's systematic choice.*

**Character: why flat characters have depth.** Narratology says that many of Dickens's flat characters give an impression of depth (P3), but does not say where the impression comes from. *The corpus evidence of as if offers a possible mechanism: what follows "as if" is a hypothetical inner life (as if he wanted my agreement, as if he did not understand); in the terms of Text World Theory, it opens an epistemic sub-world (P39). The character's inner life is not told, but implied to exist. The surface is flat; the depth is inferred by readers.*

**Generic level: Dickens reread.** Genre theory, following Tynyanov's change of function, points out that once *David Copperfield* has been rewritten (that is, reread) by *Crime and Punishment*, and *Bleak House* by Kafka's *The Trial*, Dickens's novels become something quite different from what they were before (P20, P40). *One conceivable reading: after reading *The Trial*, the endless suit in Chancery and the all-enveloping fog may be seen as a forerunner of a Kafkaesque bureaucratic labyrinth, not merely a satire on Victorian justice. Dickens himself has not changed; what has changed is the system into which he is placed.*

**Agreement and conflict: two opposite operations.** Corpus study and rereading perform two opposite operations on "Dickens's style". The corpus fixes Dickens within his own complete works and his contemporaries, measuring his deviation against a synchronic reference; rereading moves him into later systems, letting his function change with the system. The former stabilizes, the latter displaces. Stylistics itself stresses that corpus research should be guided by questions about language, characterization and the construction of fictional worlds, rather than letting "the computer has spoken" become the end of research. The two operations do not contradict each other; they correspond to the two subscripts of the verdict of deviation in P40: reference point and time.

**Conclusion:** Dickens brings each of the three sets of tools up against its own limits. Narratology can separate two Pips, two kinds of causality and a retrospective gap, but needs focalization and generic schemas to explain why the gap is not noticed; stylistics can take apart the grammar of the fog, but needs narratology's pause and panorama and genre theory's analysis of headlines to locate the meaning of these choices; the corpus can confirm the impression of "characterizing from the outside", but needs the concept of words of estrangement to explain its function in narration. Every judgement has its own level, and the power of Dickens's texts comes from the layering of these levels.

## P45 Hemingway: How Does a Restrained Style Produce Meaning?

Hemingway's style is often called "flat", "dry", "restrained" or "journalistic". Taken together, the tools of the three fields lead to a common conclusion: restraint does not mean the absence of evaluation; evaluation has been shifted into other channels: the dialogue scene, unspoken implicature, gaps in modality, internal foregrounding, and the alternation of modes of speech and thought presentation. The last section of this chapter presents the stylistic workshop on *The Old Man and the Sea* in full.

### "The Killers" and "Hills Like White Elephants": Scene and the Covert Narrator

**Plot:** In "The Killers", two hired killers walk into a small-town lunchroom to wait for and kill a Swede who regularly eats there, the former heavyweight boxer Ole Andreson; the boy Nick runs to warn him, but Ole lies on his bed and will not flee. In "Hills Like White Elephants", an American man and a girl wait for a train at a small station in the Ebro valley in Spain, talking about an "operation" that is never named.

**Text level: scene.** In scene, story duration and text duration are conventionally treated as equal, and the purest form of scene is dialogue. The exchange between the killers and the owner at the opening of "The Killers" is narratology's example (P4):

> 'I'll have a roast pork tenderloin with apple sauce and mashed potatoes,' the first man said. / 'It isn't ready yet.'

Writing made up only of dialogue and a few "stage directions" like this looks more like a fragment of a play than of a narrative.

**Level of narration: covert does not mean absent.** "The Killers" is often praised for the covertness of its narrator, but narratology points out that the dialogue is "quoted" by someone: it is this "someone" who identifies the speakers and describes the lunchroom and the characters' appearance; and in three places the text reveals the narrator's knowledge of the past: the lunchroom had been made over from a saloon, Nick had never had a towel in his mouth before, Ole had been a heavyweight prizefighter (P7). The opening of "Hills Like White Elephants" shows the minimal marker of a narrator's presence: description of setting.

> The hills across the valley of the Ebro were long and white. On this side there was no shade and no trees and the station was between two lines of rails in the sun.

In drama or film all this would be shown directly; in narrative fiction it must be put into words, and the words belong to the narrator.

**Focalization: perceived from without.** The killers' tension is suggested only by their repeatedly looking at the clock and irritably asking questions, their inner life left to be inferred from outward behaviour (P6). On the axis of "penetration into the inner life", these two killers stand at the opposite end from Molly Bloom: seen only from without, their minds remain opaque (P3).

**Pragmatic level / reading: the unspoken "operation".** *The central event of "Hills Like White Elephants" is never named: the man says it is "an awfully simple operation", "not really an operation at all". Readers infer from the evasions of the dialogue and from cultural knowledge that it is an abortion. In the classification of P39, this is a foregrounded gap that nevertheless depends on schema defaults to be filled; with the tools of P28, the man's repeated "simple" and "it's nothing" put pressure on the maxims of quantity and quality, while the girl's irony and her final request with seven pleases in a row ("Would you please please please please please please please stop talking?") shift evaluation into repetition. Repetition is among the evaluative devices Labov lists (P34).*

**Generic level: drama within narrative.** Genre theory treats "telling" and theatrical presentation as different radicals of presentation (P16). A short story made up almost entirely of dialogue calls on the dramatic radical of presentation within a narrative genre. It approaches the dramatic form in which, as Stephen says, the artist is "refined out of existence" (P43), yet it proves exactly narratology's claim: the narrator can be extremely covert but cannot vanish, because the words that identify speakers and describe the setting still need someone to utter them.

**Agreement and conflict: where has evaluation gone?** The three sets of tools give a consistent answer here. Narratology says that the narrator's perceptibility is extremely low but not zero; stylistics says that the modality of these texts is neutral; P34 has already pointed out that literary narratives with covert narrators read as if "lacking evaluation" because evaluation has been shifted into channels such as internal foregrounding, repetition and unfinished dialogue. The two stories show two kinds of shift: "The Killers" moves evaluation onto characters' outward behaviour (looking at the clock, asking questions), "Hills Like White Elephants" onto the pragmatic structure of the dialogue (evasion, irony, repetition).

### Neutral Shading and External Focalization

**Recap:** Neutral shading means the absence of modal markers in narration; what it corresponds to is not "external focalization" in the narratological sense but "the focalized perceived from without": external focalization ≠ perceived from without (P35).

**Example: a passage from *In Our Time*.**

> We were in a garden in Mons. Young Buckley came in with his patrol from across the river. The first German I saw climbed up over the garden wall. We waited till he got one leg over and then potted him. \[…\] Then three more came over further down the wall. We shot them. They all came just like that.

This is first-person narration, with no modal verbs, no evaluative adjectives, and no verbs of perception apart from saw. The sentences are short, coordinate and arranged in time order. By the classification of stylistics it is neutral shading; by the classification of narratology, however, the narrator is a participant within the story, hardly a case of "perceived from without".

**Linguistic level: where evaluation leaks out.** *Neutral shading does not mean the complete absence of attitude. Potted is a hunting colloquialism, speaking of killing a man as of shooting a bird; "They all came just like that" closes a massacre with a flat generalization.
